Abstract.

This article describes the geometry of isomorphisms between complements of geometrically irreducible curves in the affine plane 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, over an arbitrary field, which do not extend to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

We show that these isomorphisms are quite exceptional. In particular, they occur only when both curves are isomorphic to open subsets of the affine line 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. Moreover, the isomorphism is uniquely determined by one of the curves, up to post-composition by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, except in the case where the curve is isomorphic to the affine line 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} or to the punctured line 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}. Finally, we prove that when one curve is isomorphic to a line, then both curves are equivalent to lines and that when one curve is isomorphic to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}, then both curves are isomorphic to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}. In addition we provide arbitrarily many non-equivalent embeddings of the punctured line (even infinitely many in characteristic 0) with isomorphic complements.

We also give a construction that provides a large family of examples of non-isomorphic curves of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} having isomorphic complements, answering negatively to the Complement Problem raised by Hanspeter Kraft [Kra96]. This yields besides a negative answer to the holomorphic version of this problem in any dimension n≥2n\geq 2.

1. Introduction

In the Bourbaki Seminar Challenging problems on affine nn-space [Kra96] , Hanspeter Kraft gives a list of eight basic problems related to the affine nn-spaces. The sixth one is the following:

Complement Problem. Given two irreducible hypersurfaces E,F⊂𝔸nE,F\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{n} and an isomorphism of their complements, does it follow that EE and FF are isomorphic?

Recently, Pierre-Marie Poloni gave a negative answer to the problem for any n≥3n\geq 3 [Pol16]. The construction is given by explicit formulas. There are examples where both EE and FF are smooth, and examples where EE is singular, but FF is smooth. This article deals with the case of dimension n=2n=2. As we explain now (Theorem 1 below), the situation is much more rigid than in dimension n≥3n\geq 3.

We recall that two curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} are equivalent if there is an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} that sends one onto the other, and that a line C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} is a closed curve of degree 11. A variety defined over any field k\mathrm{k} is called geometrically irreducible if it is irreducible over the algebraic closure of k\mathrm{k}.

Theorem 1.

Let k\mathrm{k} be any field. Let C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be a geometrically irreducible closed curve and let φ:𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D be an isomorphism, where D⊂𝔸2D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} is also a closed curve.

If φ\varphi extends to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, then CC is sent onto DD. In particular, CC and DD are equivalent, and thus isomorphic.

If φ\varphi does not extend to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, then both CC and DD are isomorphic to open subsets of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. More precisely, we have isomorphisms

C≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])andD≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1Q])C\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}])\quad\text{and}\quad D\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}])

for some polynomials P,Q∈k⁡[t]P,Q\in\mathrm{k}[t] without square factors having the same number of roots in k\mathrm{k}, and also having the same number of roots in the algebraic closure k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}.

Moreover, the following holds:

  1. (1)(1)

    If CC is isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, then both CC and DD are equivalent to lines.

  2. (2)(2)

    If CC is not isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} or to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}, the isomorphism φ\varphi ((not extending to an automorphism of OPEN𝔸2){\mathbb{A}}^{2}) is uniquely determined by CC, up to post-composition by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. In particular, there are at most two equivalence classes of curves in 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} having complements isomorphic to 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C.

Corollary.

If the ground field k\mathrm{k} is algebraically closed, and

φ:𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D

is an isomorphism between the complements of two irreducible plane closed curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} which does not extend to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, then there exist two finite subsets F,GF,G of the affine line 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} of the same cardinality such that CC is isomorphic to 𝔸1∖F{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus F and DD is isomorphic to 𝔸1∖G{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus G.

If FF contains at least 22 points, then φ\varphi is uniquely determined by CC, up to post-composition by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. The equivalence class of DD is uniquely determined by CC, when FF is empty or contains at least 22 points.

Theorem 1 shows in particular that the Complement Problem for n=2n=2 has a positive answer if one of the curves is singular, contrary to the case where n≥3n\geq 3, as explained before. It is also very different to the case of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, where there exist non-isomorphic irreducible curves having isomorphic complements [Bla09, Theorem 1], but where all possible examples have to be singular (see Lemma 5.5 below).

Theorem 1 also shows that the Complement Problem for n=2n=2 has a positive answer if the curve is not rational (which is an easy observation, see Corollary 2.8 below) but more generally when it is not isomorphic to an open subset of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. Note that the real circle x2+y2=1x^{2}+y^{2}=1 over ℝ{\mathbb{R}} is an example of a smooth rational affine curve which is not isomorphic to an open subset of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. More precisely, Theorem 1 shows that if a curve C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} yields a negative answer to the Complement problem, then there is only one non-isomorphic curve D⊂𝔸2D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} with 𝔸2∖C≃𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\simeq{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D, and that over the algebraic closure of k\mathrm{k} the two curves are isomorphic to complements of finite subsets of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, both finite subsets having the same cardinality r≥3r\geq 3, as explained in the corollary.

Theorem 1 also gives strong restrictions on isomorphisms between complements of curves: if CC is not isomorphic to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\} and there exists an isomorphism φ:𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D not extending to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, then φ\varphi is unique (of course up to left composition by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}), hence the class of DD too. This is again quite different to the case of dimension n≥3n\geq 3 where there are infinitely many hypersurfaces E⊂𝔸nE\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{n}, up to equivalence, having isomorphic complements [Pol16, Lemma 3.1]. It is also different to the case of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, where we can find algebraic families of non-equivalent curves of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} having the same complement and thus infinitely many if k\mathrm{k} is infinite: This follows from a construction made in [Cos12], see Corollary 5.7 below.

All tools necessary to obtain the rigidity result (Theorem 1) are developped in Section 2. The proof is then achieved at the end of the section. Our second statement is the following existence result, which shows the optimality of Theorem 1.

Theorem 2.

Let k\mathrm{k} be any field.

  1. (1)(1)

    There exists a closed curve C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, isomorphic to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}, whose complement 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C admits infinitely many open embeddings 𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} into the affine plane, up to automorphisms of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. Moreover, the set of equivalence classes of such curves CC is infinite.

  2. (2)(2)

    For each integer n≥1n\geq 1 there exist curves C1,…,Cn⊂𝔸2C_{1},\dots,C_{n}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, all isomorphic to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}, no two being equivalent, such that all open surfaces 𝔸2∖C1{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{1}, …\dots, 𝔸2∖Cn{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{n} are isomorphic. If char⁡(k)=0\mathrm{char}(\mathrm{k})=0, we can moreover find an infinite sequence of curves Ci⊂𝔸2C_{i}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}, pairwise non-equivalent, such that all open surfaces 𝔸2∖Ci{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{i}, i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}, are isomorphic.

  3. (3)(3)

    For each polynomial f∈k⁡[t]f\in\mathrm{k}[t] of degree ≥1\geq 1, there exist two closed curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, both isomorphic to Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1f])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{f}]), but not equivalent, such that the open surfaces 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C and 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D are isomorphic. Moreover, the set of such pairs of closed embeddings of Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1f])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{f}]), up to equivalence, is infinite.

The proof of Theorem 2, mainly via explicit constructions, is made in Section 3.

We then give counterexamples to the Complement Problem in dimension 22, over any field:

Theorem 3.

For each ground field k\mathrm{k}, there exist two geometrically irreducible closed curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} which are not isomorphic but whose complements 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C and 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D are isomorphic. Furthermore, these two curves can be chosen of degree 77 if the field admits strictly more than 22 elements and of degree 1313 if the field has 22 elements.

The proof of this result is detailed in Section 4. We first give a geometric construction in Proposition 4.1. Then, we show in Corollary 4.2 that this construction yields, for each polynomial P∈k⁡[t]P\in\mathrm{k}[t] of degree d≥1d\geq 1 and each λ∈k\lambda\in\mathrm{k} with P⁡(λ)≠0P(\lambda)\not=0, two closed curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} of degree d2−d+1d^{2}-d+1 such that 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C and 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D are isomorphic and such that the following isomorphisms hold:

C≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])​ and ​D≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1Q]), where ​Q​(t)=P⁡(λ+1t)⋅tdeg⁡(P).C\simeq\Spec\Big(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}]\Big)\text{ and }D\simeq\Spec\Big(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}]\Big),\text{ where }Q(t)=P\Big(\lambda+\frac{1}{t}\Big)\cdot t^{\deg(P)}.

The proof of Theorem 3 follows by providing an appropriate pair (P,λ)(P,\lambda) for each field. The case of infinite fields is quite easy. Indeed, if k\mathrm{k} is infinite and P∈k⁡[t]P\in\mathrm{k}[t] is a polynomial having at least 33 roots in k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}, then Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}]) and Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1Q])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}]) are not isomorphic, when Q⁡(t)=P⁡(λ+1t)⋅tdeg⁡(P)Q(t)=P(\lambda+\frac{1}{t})\cdot t^{\deg(P)} and λ∈k\lambda\in\mathrm{k} is a general element, so we can find two curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} having isomorphic complements, such that CC is isomorphic to Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}]) but not DD (Corollary 4.4). This shows that the isomorphism type of counterexamples to the Complement Problem is as large as possible.

We finish this introduction by giving some easy implications of Theorem 3, detailed in Section 5:

(i)(i) The negative answer to the Complement Problem for n=2n=2 directly yields a negative answer for any n≥3n\geq 3 (Lemma 5.1): Our construction gives, for each n≥3n\geq 3, two geometrically irreducible smooth closed hypersurfaces E,F⊂𝔸nE,F\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{n} which are not isomorphic but whose complements 𝔸n∖E{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\setminus E and 𝔸n∖F{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\setminus F are isomorphic (Corollary 5.2). All the hypersurfaces provided this way are isomorphic to 𝔸n−2×C{\mathbb{A}}^{n-2}\times C for some open subset C⊂𝔸1C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. This does not allow to give singular examples like the ones of [Pol16], but gives a different type of examples.

(i​i)(ii) Choosing k=ℂ\mathrm{k}={\mathbb{C}}, our construction also gives families of closed complex curves C,D⊂ℂ2C,D\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{2} such that ℂ2∖C{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\setminus C and ℂ2∖D{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\setminus D are biholomorphic (because they are isomorphic as algebraic varieties) but CC and DD are not biholomorphic (Lemma 5.3). This directly provides, for each n≥2n\geq 2, the existence of algebraic hypersurfaces H1,H2⊂ℂnH_{1},H_{2}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{n} which are complex manifolds, not biholomorphic but having biholomorphic complements (Corollary 5.4). This is, to our knowledge, the first family of such examples, and yields the answer to a problem asked in [Pol16]. Note that in the counterexamples of [Pol16], if both hypersurfaces are smooth, then they are always biholomorphic (even if they are not isomorphic as algebraic varieties).

2. Geometric description of open embeddings 𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2}

In the sequel, we work over a field k\mathrm{k}, which is a priori any field (except when we precise the field). When we say rational, resp. isomorphic, we mean k\mathrm{k}-rational, resp. k\mathrm{k}-isomorphic. The word geometrically rational or geometrically irreducible refers to the extension to the algebraic closure k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}, as usual.

2.1. Basic properties

In order to study isomorphisms between affine surfaces, it is often interesting to see the affine surfaces as open subsets of projective surfaces and to see then the isomorphisms as birational maps between the projective surfaces. The aim of this section is to establish Lemma 2.7, that we use often in the sequel. Its proof relies on some easy results that we recall before: Lemmas 2.2, 2.4, 2.6 and Corollary 2.5.

Example 2.1.

The morphism

𝔸2↪ℙ2(x,y)↦[x:y:1]\begin{array}[]{rcl}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}&\hookrightarrow&{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\\ (x,y)&\mapsto&[x:y:1]\end{array}

gives an isomorphism 𝔸2⟶≃ℙ2∖Lℙ2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}, where Lℙ2⊂ℙ2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{2} denotes the “line at infinity” given by z=0z=0. The above embedding of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} into ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} will be often used in the sequel, and called the standard embedding.

With this standard embedding, every line of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, given by an equation a​x+b​y=cax+by=c where a,b,ca,b,c are elements of k\mathrm{k} and a,ba,b are not both zero, is the restriction of a line of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, given by the equation a​x+b​y=c​zax+by=cz, and distinct from Lℙ2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}.

Lemma 2.2.

Let φ:X⇢Y\varphi\colon X\dasharrow Y be a birational map between two projective surfaces and assume that φ\varphi restricts to an isomorphism U⟶≃VU\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}V where U⊂XU\subset X and V⊂YV\subset Y are two open subsets. Then, any geometrically irreducible closed curve Γ⊂X∖U\Gamma\subset X\setminus U is sent either to a point of Y∖VY\setminus V or to a curve contained in Y∖VY\setminus V.

Proof.

The minimal resolution of φ\varphi yields a commutative diagram

where η\eta and π\pi blow up respectively the base-points of φ\varphi and φ−1\varphi^{-1}, which are by assumption not contained in UU and VV respectively. This yields η−1​(U)=π−1​(V)\eta^{-1}(U)=\pi^{-1}(V), which implies the result. ∎

Definition 2.3.

For each birational φ:ℙ2⇢ℙ2\varphi\colon{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, one defines Jφ⊂ℙ2J_{\varphi}\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{2} to be the reduced curve given by the union of all irreducible k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-curves contracted by φ\varphi.

Lemma 2.4.

Let φ:ℙ2⇢ℙ2\varphi\colon{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2} be a birational map.

  1. (1)(1)

    The curve JφJ_{\varphi} is defined over k\mathrm{k}, i.e. is the zero locus of a homogeneous polynomial f∈k⁡[x,y,z]f\in\mathrm{k}[x,y,z].

  2. (2)(2)

    We have an isomorphism ℙ2∖Jφ→ℙ2∖Jφ−1{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus J_{\varphi}\to{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus J_{\varphi^{-1}}. Moreover, the number of k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-irreducible components of JφJ_{\varphi} and Jφ−1J_{\varphi^{-1}} are equal.

Proof.

(1): If char⁡(k)=0\mathrm{char}(\mathrm{k})=0 one could choose ff to be the Jacobian determinant associated to φ\varphi. This does not work in positive characteristic as the Jacobian determinant can be zero. We then do as follows: we write φ\varphi as φ:[x:y:z]↦[s0(x,y,z):s1(x,y,z):s2(x,y,z)]\varphi\colon[x:y:z]\mapsto[s_{0}(x,y,z):s_{1}(x,y,z):s_{2}(x,y,z)], where s0,s1,s2∈k⁡[x,y,z]s_{0},s_{1},s_{2}\in\mathrm{k}[x,y,z] are homogeneous polynomials of the same degree without common factor and do the same with φ−1:[x:y:z]↦[q0(x,y,z):q1(x,y,z):q2(x,y,z)]\varphi^{-1}\colon[x:y:z]\mapsto[q_{0}(x,y,z):q_{1}(x,y,z):q_{2}(x,y,z)]. We then do the composition and obtain q0​(s0,s1,s2)=x​Aq_{0}(s_{0},s_{1},s_{2})=xA, q1​(s0,s1,s2)=y​Aq_{1}(s_{0},s_{1},s_{2})=yA, q2​(s0,s1,s2)=z​Aq_{2}(s_{0},s_{1},s_{2})=zA, for some polynomial A∈k⁡[x,y,z]A\in\mathrm{k}[x,y,z] and observe that JφJ_{\varphi} is the zero locus of AA. Indeed, the polynomial AA is zero along an irreducible k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-curve if and only if this curve is sent by φ\varphi onto a base-point of φ−1\varphi^{-1}.

(2)(\ref{IsoJvarphi}) We take a minimal resolution of φ\varphi, which yields a commutative diagram

where η\eta and π\pi are birational morphisms, the morphism η\eta, resp. π\pi, being the sequence of blow-ups of the k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-base-points of φ{\varphi}, resp. φ−1\varphi^{-1}.

We can now work over k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}, forgetting the subfield k\mathrm{k}. Computing the Picard rank of XX, we see that η\eta and π\pi contract the same number of irreducible curves of XX. Let nn be this number. We then denote by E⊂XE\subset X, resp. F⊂XF\subset X, the union of the nn irreducible curves contracted by η\eta, resp. π\pi. The map φ\varphi restricts then to an isomorphism

ℙ2∖η⁡(E∪F)⟶≃ℙ2∖π⁡(E∪F){\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus\eta(E\cup F)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus\pi(E\cup F)

Let us observe that η⁡(E∪F)=η⁡(F)\eta(E\cup F)=\eta(F). Since η⁡(E)\eta(E) consists of finitely many points, it suffices to show that these are contained in the curves of η⁡(F)\eta(F). Each point pp of η⁡(E)\eta(E) corresponds to a connected component of EE, which contains at least one (−1)(-1)-curve ℰ⊂E\mathcal{E}\subset E. The curve ℰ\mathcal{E} is not contracted by π\pi, by minimality, hence sent by π\pi onto a curve π⁡(ℰ)⊂ℙ2\pi(\mathcal{E})\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, of self-intersection ≥1\geq 1. This implies that ℰ\mathcal{E} intersects FF and thus p∈η⁡(F)p\in\eta(F). One similarly gets π⁡(E∪F)=π⁡(E)\pi(E\cup F)=\pi(E), and obtains that φ\varphi restricts to an isomorphism

ℙ2∖η⁡(F)⟶≃ℙ2∖π⁡(E).{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus\eta(F)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus\pi(E).

It remains to observe that η⁡(F)\eta(F) is a closed curve of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} (in general not irreducible) and that each of its k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-component is contracted by φ\varphi, so η⁡(F)=Jφ\eta(F)=J_{\varphi}. Similarly, one gets π⁡(E)=Jφ−1\pi(E)=J_{\varphi^{-1}}. Moreover, the number of k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-irreducible components of η⁡(F)\eta(F) is equal to the number of k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-irreducible components of F∖E¯\overline{F\setminus E}, which is equal to the number of k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-irreducible components of E∖F¯\overline{E\setminus F}. This achieves the proof. ∎

Corollary 2.5.

Let φ:ℙ2∖Γ↪ℙ2\varphi\colon{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus\Gamma\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2} be an open embedding, where Γ\Gamma is a closed k\mathrm{k}-curve, which is a finite union of rr distinct irreducible closed k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-curves of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}. Then, there is a unique closed k\mathrm{k}-curve Δ⊂ℙ2\Delta\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{2} such that φ⁡(ℙ2∖Γ)=ℙ2∖Δ\varphi({\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus\Gamma)={\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus\Delta, and Δ\Delta is also a finite union of rr distinct irreducible closed k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-curves of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}.

Proof.

Let φ^:ℙ2⇢ℙ2\hat{\varphi}\colon{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2} be the birational map induced by φ\varphi. Lemma 2.4 implies that Jφ^⊂ΓJ_{\hat{\varphi}}\subset\Gamma, that Jφ^J_{\hat{\varphi}} and Jφ^−1J_{\hat{\varphi}^{-1}} are finite unions of s≤rs\leq r irreducible closed distinct k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-curves of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, and that φ^\hat{\varphi} induces an isomorphism ℙ2∖Jφ^⟶≃ℙ2∖Jφ^−1.{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus J_{\hat{\varphi}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus J_{\hat{\varphi}^{-1}}.

If s=rs=r, the proof is over. Otherwise, Γ′=Γ∖Jφ^\Gamma^{\prime}=\Gamma\setminus J_{\hat{\varphi}} is a closed k\mathrm{k}-curve of ℙ2∖Jφ^{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus J_{\hat{\varphi}}, which is the union of r−sr-s irreducible closed k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-curves. The closed k\mathrm{k}-curve Δ′=φ^​(Γ′)\Delta^{\prime}=\hat{\varphi}(\Gamma^{\prime}) of ℙ2∖Jφ^−1{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus J_{\hat{\varphi}^{-1}} is again the union of r−sr-s irreducible closed k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-curves. The result follows with Δ=Δ′∪Jφ^−1\Delta=\Delta^{\prime}\cup J_{\hat{\varphi}^{-1}}. ∎

Lemma 2.6.

Let φ:X⇢Y\varphi\colon X\dasharrow Y be a birational map between two smooth projective surfaces ((all defined over 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁k)\mathrm{k}), such that every irreducible k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-curve contracted by φ\varphi is defined over k\mathrm{k}. Then, each base-point of φ−1\varphi^{-1} is k\mathrm{k}-rational and each curve contracted by φ\varphi is k\mathrm{k}-rational.

Proof.

We argue by induction on the number of base-points of φ−1\varphi^{-1}. If there is no such base-point, there is nothing to show. Otherwise, let CC be an irreducible k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-curve contracted by φ\varphi onto a point pp of YY. Since CC is defined over k\mathrm{k}, so is its image, i.e. pp is k\mathrm{k}-rational (the generic point of CC is defined over k\mathrm{k} and is sent onto the k\mathrm{k}-point pp). Let π:Y′→Y\pi\colon Y^{\prime}\to Y be the blow-up at pp and let φ′=π−1∘φ:X⇢Y′\varphi^{\prime}=\pi^{-1}\circ\varphi\colon X\dasharrow Y^{\prime}. The base-points of (φ′)−1(\varphi^{\prime})^{-1} coincide with the base-points of φ−1\varphi^{-1} from which the point pp is removed. Moreover, the curves contracted by φ′\varphi^{\prime} are also contracted by φ\varphi, and if a curve is contracted by φ\varphi and not contracted by φ′\varphi^{\prime}, then it is sent by φ′\varphi^{\prime} onto the exceptional divisor π−1​(p)\pi^{-1}(p) and is thus k\mathrm{k}-rational. Therefore, the result follows by induction. ∎

In the sequel, we will constantly use the following observation:

Lemma 2.7.

Let C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be a geometrically irreducible closed curve and let φ:𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be an open embedding. Then, there exists a geometrically irreducible closed curve D⊂𝔸2D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} such that φ⁡(𝔸2∖C)=𝔸2∖D\varphi({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)={\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D. Denote by C¯\overline{C} and D¯\overline{D} the closures of CC and DD in ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, denote as in Example 2.1 by Lℙ2=ℙ2∖𝔸2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}={\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus{\mathbb{A}}^{2} the line at infinity and denote by φ^:ℙ2⇢ℙ2\hat{\varphi}\colon{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2} the birational map induced by φ\varphi. Then, one of the following three alternatives holds:

  1. (1)(1)

    We have φ^​(C¯)=D¯\hat{\varphi}(\overline{C})=\overline{D}. Then, the map φ\varphi extends to an automorphism of 𝔸2=ℙ2∖Lℙ2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}={\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}} sending CC onto DD.

  2. (2)(2)

    We have φ^​(C¯)=Lℙ2\hat{\varphi}(\overline{C})=L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}. Then, the curve DD is a line of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, i.e. D¯\overline{D} is a line of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} and φ\varphi extends to an isomorphism from 𝔸2=ℙ2∖Lℙ2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}={\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}} to ℙ2∖D¯{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus\overline{D}, that sends CC onto Lℙ2∖D¯L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\setminus\overline{D}. In particular, CC is equivalent to a line via an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

  3. (3)(3)

    The map φ^\hat{\varphi} contracts the curve C¯\overline{C} onto a k\mathrm{k}-point of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}. Then, the curve C¯\overline{C} (and therefore, also the curve CC) is a rational curve ((i.e. is k\mathrm{k}-birational to ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1})).

Proof.

The restriction of φ^\hat{\varphi} to ℙ2∖(Lℙ2∪C¯)=𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus(L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\cup\overline{C})={\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C gives the open embedding φ:𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2↪ℙ2\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2}. By Corollary 2.5, we obtain an isomorphism ℙ2∖(Lℙ2∪C¯)⟶≃ℙ2∖Δ{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus(L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\cup\overline{C})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus\Delta, for some k\mathrm{k}-curve Δ⊂ℙ2\Delta\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, which is the union of two k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-irreducible closed curves of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}. Since Lℙ2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}} is included in Δ\Delta, there exists an irreducible closed k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-curve DD of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} such that Δ=Lℙ2∪D¯\Delta=L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\cup\overline{D}. As a conclusion, φ^\hat{\varphi} induces an isomorphism

ℙ2∖(Lℙ2∪C¯)⟶≃ℙ2∖(Lℙ2∪D¯).{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus(L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\cup\overline{C})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus(L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\cup\overline{D}).

It follows that φ⁡(𝔸2∖C)=𝔸2∖D\varphi({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)={\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D. The equality D=𝔸2∖φ⁡(𝔸2∖C)D={\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus\varphi({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C) proves us that the curve DD is defined over k\mathrm{k} and is therefore geometrically irreducible. By Lemma 2.2, one of the following three alternatives holds:

  1. (1)

    We have φ^​(C¯)=D¯\hat{\varphi}(\overline{C})=\overline{D}. Hence, φ^\hat{\varphi} induces an automorphism of 𝔸2=ℙ2∖Lℙ2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}={\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}} (Lemma 2.4).

  2. (2)

    We have φ^​(C¯)=Lℙ2\hat{\varphi}(\overline{C})=L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}. Then, φ^\hat{\varphi} induces an isomorphism ℙ2∖Lℙ2⟶≃ℙ2∖D¯{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus\overline{D} (again by Lemma 2.4). Since the Picard group of ℙ2∖Γ{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus\Gamma is isomorphic to ℤ/deg⁡(Γ)​ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}/\deg(\Gamma){\mathbb{Z}}, for each irreducible curve Γ\Gamma, the curve D¯\overline{D} must be a line of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}.

  3. (3)

    The map φ^\hat{\varphi} contracts the curve C¯\overline{C} onto a point of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}. Then, by Lemma 2.6, this point is necessary a k\mathrm{k}-point and the curve C¯\overline{C} is k\mathrm{k}-rational. ∎

Corollary 2.8.

Let C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be a geometrically irreducible closed curve. If CC is not rational ((i.e. not k\mathrm{k}-birational to 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁ℙ1){\mathbb{P}}^{1}), then every open embedding 𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} extends to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

Proof.

Follows from Lemma 2.7 and the fact that cases (2)-(3) only occur when CC is rational. ∎

Remark 2.9.

It follows from Corollary 2.8 that the group of automorphisms of 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C, where CC is a non-rational geometrically irreducible curve, is the subgroup of Aut⁡(𝔸2)\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{2}) preserving CC. By [BS15, Theorem 2], this group is finite (and in particular conjugate to a subgroup of GL2⁡(k)\GL_{2}(\mathrm{k}) if char⁡(k)=0\mathrm{char}(\mathrm{k})=0, see for instance [Kam79]).

We find it interesting to observe that case (3) of Lemma 2.7 only occurs when C¯\overline{C} intersects Lℙ2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}} in at most two k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-points, even if this will not be used in the sequel.

Corollary 2.10.

If C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} is a closed geometrically irreducible curve such that C¯\overline{C} intersects Lℙ2=ℙ2∖𝔸2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}={\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus{\mathbb{A}}^{2} in at least three k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-points, then every open embedding 𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} extends to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

Proof.

We can assume that k=k¯\mathrm{k}=\overline{\mathrm{k}}. Suppose, for contradiction, that the extension φ^:ℙ2⇢ℙ2\hat{\varphi}\colon{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2} does not restrict to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. By Lemma 2.7, the curve C¯\overline{C} is contracted by φ^\hat{\varphi} (because CC is not equivalent to a line, so (2) is impossible). We recall that φ^\hat{\varphi} restricts to an isomorphism 𝔸2∖C=ℙ2∖(Lℙ2∪C¯)⟶≃𝔸2∖D=ℙ2∖(Lℙ2∪D¯){\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C={\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus(L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\cup\overline{C})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D={\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus(L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\cup\overline{D}) (Lemma 2.7) and that C¯⊂Jφ^⊂Lℙ2∪C¯\overline{C}\subset J_{\hat{\varphi}}\subset L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\cup\overline{C}, Jφ^−1⊂Lℙ2∪D¯J_{\hat{\varphi}^{-1}}\subset L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\cup\overline{D}, where Jφ^J_{\hat{\varphi}}, Jφ^−1J_{\hat{\varphi}^{-1}} have the same number of irreducible components (Lemma 2.4). We take a minimal resolution of φ^\hat{\varphi}, which yields a commutative diagram

We first observe that the strict transforms L~ℙ2,C~⊂X\tilde{L}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}},\tilde{C}\subset X of Lℙ2,C¯L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}},\overline{C} by η\eta intersect in at most one point. Secondly, the fact that L~ℙ2,C~⊂X\tilde{L}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}},\tilde{C}\subset X intersect in at most one point implies that η\eta blows up all points of C¯∩Lℙ2\overline{C}\cap L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}} except at most one. Remark 2.11.

In case (3) of Lemma 2.7, it is possible that C¯\overline{C} intersects the line Lℙ2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}} in two points, as it is the case in most of our examples (see for example Lemma 3.1 or Lemma 3.7). The case of one point is of course also possible (see for instance Lemma 2.13(1)).

We will also need the following basic algebraic observation.

Lemma 2.12.

Let f∈k⁡[x,y]f\in\mathrm{k}[x,y] be a polynomial, irreducible over k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}, and let C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be the curve given by f=0f=0. Then, the ring of functions on 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C and its subset of invertible elements are equal to

𝒪(𝔸2∖C)=k[x,y,f−1]⊂k(x,y),𝒪(𝔸2∖C)∗={λfn∣λ∈k∗,n∈ℤ}.\mathcal{O}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)=\mathrm{k}[x,y,f^{-1}]\subset\mathrm{k}(x,y),\ \mathcal{O}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)^{*}=\{\lambda f^{n}\mid\lambda\in\mathrm{k}^{*},n\in\mathbb{Z}\}.

In particular, every automorphism of 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C exchanges the fibres of the morphism

𝔸2∖C→𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}

given by ff.

Proof.

The field of rational functions of 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C is equal to k⁡(x,y)\mathrm{k}(x,y). We can write any element of this field as uv\frac{u}{v}, where u,v∈k⁡[x,y]u,v\in\mathrm{k}[x,y] are coprime polynomials, v≠0v\not=0. The rational function is regular on 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C if and only if vv does not vanish on any k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-point of 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C. This means that v=λ​fnv=\lambda f^{n}, for some λ∈k∗\lambda\in\mathrm{k}^{*}, n≥0n\geq 0. This provides the description of 𝒪⁡(𝔸2∖C)\mathcal{O}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C) and 𝒪​(𝔸2∖C)∗\mathcal{O}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)^{*}. The last remark follows from the fact that 𝒪​(𝔸2∖C)∗\mathcal{O}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)^{*} is generated by k∗\mathrm{k}^{*} and one element, if and only if this element is λ​f±1\lambda f^{\pm 1} for some λ∈k∗\lambda\in\mathrm{k}^{*}. ∎

2.2. The case of lines

Lemma 2.7 shows that one needs to study isomorphisms 𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D, which extend to birational maps of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} that contract the curve CC onto a point. One can ask whether this point can be a point of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} (and thus would be contained in DD) or belongs to the boundary line Lℙ2=ℙ2∖𝔸2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}={\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. As we will show (Corollary 2.19), the first possibility only occurs in a very special case, namely when CC is equivalent to a line by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. The case of lines is special for this reason, and is treated separately here.

Lemma 2.13.

Let C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be the line given by x=0x=0.

  1. (1)(1)

    The group of automorphisms of 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C is given by:

    Aut(𝔸2∖C)={(x,y)↦(λx±1,μxny+s(x,x−1))∣λ,μ∈k∗,n∈ℤ,s∈k[x,x−1]}.\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)=\{(x,y)\mapsto(\lambda x^{\pm 1},\mu x^{n}y+s(x,x^{-1}))\mid\lambda,\mu\in\mathrm{k}^{*},n\in{\mathbb{Z}},s\in\mathrm{k}[x,x^{-1}]\}.
  2. (2)(2)

    Every open embedding 𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} is equal to ψ​α\psi\alpha, where α∈Aut⁡(𝔸2∖C)\alpha\in\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C) and ψ:𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2\psi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} extends to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. In particular, the complement of its image, i.e. the complement of ψ​α​(𝔸2∖C)=ψ⁡(𝔸2∖C)\psi\alpha({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)=\psi({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C), is a curve equivalent to a line by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

Proof.

To prove (1), we first observe that each transformation (x,y)↦(λ​x±1,μ​xn​y+s⁡(x,x−1))(x,y)\mapsto(\lambda x^{\pm 1},\mu x^{n}y+s(x,x^{-1})) actually yields an automorphism of 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C. Then, we only need to show that all automorphisms of 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C are of this form. An automorphism of 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C corresponds to an automorphism of k⁡[x,y,x−1]\mathrm{k}[x,y,x^{-1}], which sends xx onto λ​x±1\lambda x^{\pm 1}, where λ∈k∗\lambda\in\mathrm{k}^{*} (Lemma 2.12). Applying the inverse of (x,y)↦(λ​x±1,y)(x,y)\mapsto(\lambda x^{\pm 1},y), we can assume that xx is fixed. We are left with an RR-automorphism of R⁡[y]R[y], where RR is the ring k⁡[x,x−1]\mathrm{k}[x,x^{-1}]. Such an automorphism is of the form y↦a​y+by\mapsto ay+b, where a∈R∗a\in R^{*}, b∈Rb\in R. Indeed, if the maps y↦p⁡(y)y\mapsto p(y) and y↦q⁡(y)y\mapsto q(y) are inverses of each other, the equality y=p⁡(q⁡(y))y=p(q(y)) proves us that deg⁡p=deg⁡q=1\deg p=\deg q=1. This yields the desired form.

To prove (2), we use Lemma 2.7 and write φ\varphi as an isomorphism 𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D where DD is a geometrically irreducible closed curve, and only need to see that DD is equivalent to a line by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. We write ψ=φ−1\psi=\varphi^{-1}, choose an equation f=0f=0 for DD (where f∈k⁡[x,y]f\in\mathrm{k}[x,y] is an irreducible polynomial over k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}) and get an isomorphism ψ∗:𝒪⁡(𝔸2∖C)=k⁡[x,y,x−1]→𝒪⁡(𝔸2∖D)=k⁡[x,y,f−1]\psi^{*}\colon\mathcal{O}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)=\mathrm{k}[x,y,x^{-1}]\to\mathcal{O}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D)=\mathrm{k}[x,y,f^{-1}] that sends xx onto λ​f±1\lambda f^{\pm 1} for some λ∈k∗\lambda\in\mathrm{k}^{*} (Lemma 2.12). We can thus write ψ\psi as (x,y)↦(λ​f​(x,y)±1,g⁡(x,y)​f​(x,y)n)(x,y)\mapsto(\lambda f(x,y)^{\pm 1},g(x,y)f(x,y)^{n}), where n∈ℤn\in{\mathbb{Z}} and g∈k⁡[x,y]g\in\lx@nobreakspace\mathrm{k}[x,y]. Replacing ψ\psi with its composition with the automorphism (x,y)↦((λ−1​x)±1,y​((λ−1​x)±1)−n)(x,y)\mapsto((\lambda^{-1}x)^{\pm 1},y((\lambda^{-1}x)^{\pm 1})^{-n}) of 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C, we can assume that ψ\psi is of the form (x,y)↦(f⁡(x,y),g⁡(x,y))(x,y)\mapsto(f(x,y),g(x,y)). If gg is equal to a constant ν∈k\nu\in\mathrm{k} modulo ff, we apply the automorphism (x,y)↦(x,(y−ν)​x−1)(x,y)\mapsto(x,(y-\nu)x^{-1}) and decrease the degree of gg. After finitely many steps we obtain an isomorphism 𝔸2∖D→𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C of the form ψ0:(x,y)↦(f⁡(x,y),g⁡(x,y))\psi_{0}\colon(x,y)\mapsto(f(x,y),g(x,y)) where gg is not a constant modulo ff. The image of DD by ψ0\psi_{0} is then dense in CC, which implies that ψ0\psi_{0} extends to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} sending DD onto CC (Lemma 2.7). ∎

2.3. Embeddings into Hirzebruch surfaces

We will not only need embeddings of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} into ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} but also other embeddings of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} into smooth projective surfaces, and in particular into Hirzebruch surfaces.

Example 2.14.

For n≥1n\geq 1, the nn-th Hirzebruch surface 𝔽n{\mathbb{F}}_{n} is

𝔽n={([a:b:c],[u:v])∈ℙ2×ℙ1|bvn=cun}{\mathbb{F}}_{n}=\{([a:b:c],[u:v])\in{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\ |\ bv^{n}=cu^{n}\}

and the projection πn:𝔽n→ℙ1\pi_{n}\colon{\mathbb{F}}_{n}\to{\mathbb{P}}^{1} yields a ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-bundle structure on 𝔽n{\mathbb{F}}_{n}.

Let Sn,Fn⊂𝔽nS_{n},F_{n}\subset{\mathbb{F}}_{n} be the curves given by [1:0:0]×ℙ1[1:0:0]\times{\mathbb{P}}^{1} and v=0v=0, respectively. The morphism

𝔸2↪𝔽n(x,y)↦([x:yn:1],[y:1])\begin{array}[]{rcl}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}&\hookrightarrow&{\mathbb{F}}_{n}\\ (x,y)&\mapsto&([x:y^{n}:1],[y:1])\end{array}

2.4. Extension to regular morphisms on 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}

The following proposition, is the principal tool in the proof of Lemma 2.22, Corollary 2.23 and Proposition 2.25, which themselves give the main part of Theorem 1.

Proposition 2.17.

Let C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be a geometrically irreducible closed curve, not equivalent to a line by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, and let φ:𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be an open embedding. Then, there exists an open embedding ι:𝔸2↪𝔽n\iota\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{F}}_{n}, for some n≥1n\geq 1, such that the rational map ι∘φ\iota\circ\varphi extends to a regular morphism 𝔸2→𝔽n{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{F}}_{n}, and such that ι⁡(𝔸2)=𝔽n∖(Sn∪Fn)\iota({\mathbb{A}}^{2})={\mathbb{F}}_{n}\setminus(S_{n}\cup F_{n}) ((where SnS_{n} and FnF_{n} are as in Example 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁2.14)\ref{Exa:Hirzebruch}).

By Lemma 2.7, φ⁡(𝔸2∖C)=𝔸2∖D\varphi({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)={\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D for some geometrically irreducible curve DD. If φ\varphi extends to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} sending CC onto DD, the result is obvious, by taking any isomorphism ι:𝔸2⟶≃𝔽n∖(Fn∪Sn)\iota\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{F}}_{n}\setminus(F_{n}\cup S_{n}), so we can assume that φ\varphi does not extend to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. Lemma 2.13 implies, since CC is not equivalent to a line by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, that the same holds for DD. Moreover, Lemma 2.7 implies that the extension of φ−1\varphi^{-1} to a birational map 𝔸2⇢ℙ2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, via the standard embedding 𝔸2↪ℙ2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, contracts the curve DD (or D¯\overline{D}) onto a k\mathrm{k}-point of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}. In particular, it does not send DD birationally onto CC or onto Lℙ2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}.

We choose an open embedding ι:𝔸2↪𝔽n\iota\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{F}}_{n} given by Lemma 2.16, which comes from an isomorphism ι:𝔸2⟶≃𝔽n\(Sn∪Fn)\iota\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{F}}_{n}\backslash(S_{n}\cup F_{n}), such that the closure ι⁡(D)\iota(D) in 𝔽n{\mathbb{F}}_{n} is a curve Γ\Gamma which satisfies one of the two possibilities (1)-(2) of Lemma 2.16.

We want to show that the open embedding ι∘φ:𝔸2∖C↪𝔽n\iota\circ\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{F}}_{n} extends to a regular morphism on 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. Using the standard embedding of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} into ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, one gets a birational map ψ:ℙ2⇢𝔽n\psi\colon{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{F}}_{n} and needs to show that all base-points of this map are contained in Lℙ2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}. We take as usual a minimal resolution of ψ\psi and obtain a commutative diagram

As we observed before, the map ψ−1:𝔽n⇢ℙ2\psi^{-1}\colon{\mathbb{F}}_{n}\dasharrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2} contracts Γ=ι⁡(D)¯\Gamma=\overline{\iota(D)} onto a k\mathrm{k}-point, and thus does not send Γ\Gamma birationally onto CC or Lℙ2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}. The possible curves contracted by ψ\psi are Lℙ2,C¯L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}},\overline{C} and the possible curves contracted by ψ−1\psi^{-1} are Γ,Fn,Sn\Gamma,F_{n},S_{n}. Since all these are defined over k\mathrm{k}, all base-points of ψ,ψ−1\psi,\psi^{-1} are defined over k\mathrm{k} (Lemma 2.6).

We suppose, for contradiction, that ψ\psi has a base-point qq in 𝔸2=ℙ2∖Lℙ2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}={\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}, which means that one (−1)(-1)-curve Eq⊂XE_{q}\subset X is contracted by η\eta onto qq. The minimality of the resolution implies that π\pi does not contract EqE_{q}, so π⁡(Eq)\pi(E_{q}) is a curve of 𝔽n{\mathbb{F}}_{n} contracted by ψ−1\psi^{-1} onto qq, which belongs to {Γ,Fn,Sn}\{\Gamma,F_{n},S_{n}\}.

We observe that ψ\psi has also a base-point pp in Lℙ2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}. Indeed, otherwise the strict transform of Lℙ2L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}} would have self-intersection 11 on XX and would then not be contracted by π\pi, and would be sent onto a curve of self-intersection ≥1\geq 1, which belongs to {Γ,Fn,Sn}\{\Gamma,F_{n},S_{n}\} by Lemma 2.2. We thus have at least two of the curves Γ\Gamma, FnF_{n}, SnS_{n} that correspond to (−1)(-1)-curves of XX contracted by η\eta.

We suppose first that SnS_{n} corresponds to a (−1)(-1)-curve of XX contracted by η\eta. mr​(Γ)=Γ⋅Fn≥1m_{r}(\Gamma)=\Gamma\cdot F_{n}\geq 1 and Γ∩Fn={r}\Gamma\cap F_{n}=\{r\},

since Fn~\tilde{F_{n}} and Γ~\tilde{\Gamma} are disjoint on XX (and because Γ⋅Fn≥1\Gamma\cdot F_{n}\geq 1, as Γ\Gamma satisfies the conditions (1)-(2) of Lemma 2.16).

We now prove that π−1​(r)\pi^{-1}(r) and π−1​(Sn)\pi^{-1}(S_{n}) are two disjoint connected sets of rational curves which intersect the two curves Fn~\tilde{F_{n}} and Γ~\tilde{\Gamma}, i.e. the two curves EpE_{p} and EqE_{q}. To show this, it suffices to prove that r∉Snr\notin S_{n} and that Sn⋅Γ≥1S_{n}\cdot\Gamma\geq 1. Suppose first that Γ⋅Fn=1\Gamma\cdot F_{n}=1 (condition (1) of Lemma 2.16). Since C∩Fn∩Sn=∅C\cap F_{n}\cap S_{n}=\emptyset, we get r∈Fn∖Snr\in F_{n}\setminus S_{n}. The inequality Γ⋅Sn>0\Gamma\cdot S_{n}>0 is provided by the fact that DD is not equivalent to a line by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} (see again condition (1) of Lemma 2.16). Suppose then that Γ⋅Fn≥2\Gamma\cdot F_{n}\geq 2 (equivalence (iv)-(ii) in case (2) of Lemma 2.16). As mr​(Γ)=Γ⋅Fn≥2m_{r}(\Gamma)=\Gamma\cdot F_{n}\geq 2, we have 2​mr​(Γ)>Γ⋅Fn2m_{r}(\Gamma)>\Gamma\cdot F_{n}, which implies that n=1n=1, r∈Fn∖Snr\in F_{n}\setminus S_{n} and 2≤mr​(Γ)≤Γ⋅Sn2\leq m_{r}(\Gamma)\leq\Gamma\cdot S_{n} (see again possibility (2) of Lemma 2.16).

We finish by observing that, since η⁡(Eq)=q∈ℙ2∖Lℙ2\eta(E_{q})=q\in{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}} and η⁡(Ep)=p∈Lℙ2\eta(E_{p})=p\in L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}, any connected set of curves of η−1​(Lℙ2∪C)\eta^{-1}(L_{{\mathbb{P}}^{2}}\cup C) which touches the two curves EqE_{q} and EpE_{p} has to contain the strict transform C~\tilde{C} of C¯\overline{C}. This contradicts the fact that π−1​(r)\pi^{-1}(r) and π−1​(Sn)\pi^{-1}(S_{n}) are two disjoint connected sets of rational curves which intersect the two curves Fn~\tilde{F_{n}} and Γ~\tilde{\Gamma}. ∎

A direct corollary of Proposition 2.17 is the following, which shows that only smooth curves C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} are interesting to study. This follows also from Lemma 2.22 below. Since the proof of Lemma 2.22 is more involved, we prefer to first explain the simple argument that shows how the smoothness follows from Proposition 2.17.

Corollary 2.18.

Let C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be a geometrically irreducible curve and let φ:𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be an open embedding. If CC is not smooth, then every open embedding 𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} extends to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.7, φ⁡(𝔸2∖C)=𝔸2∖D\varphi({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)={\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D for some geometrically irreducible curve DD. We apply Proposition 2.17 and obtain an open embedding ι:𝔸2↪𝔽n\iota\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{F}}_{n}, for some n≥1n\geq 1, such that the rational map ι∘φ\iota\circ\varphi extends to a regular morphism 𝔸2→𝔽n{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{F}}_{n}. Embedding 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} into ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, we get a birational map ℙ2⇢𝔽n{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{F}}_{n} which is regular on 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. In particular, the singular points of CC are not blown up in the minimal resolution of the birational transformation ℙ2⇢𝔽n{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{F}}_{n}. So, the curve CC is not contracted. By Lemma 2.2, it is then sent onto a singular curve of 𝔽n{\mathbb{F}}_{n}, not contained in 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D. The three irreducible curves of 𝔽n{\mathbb{F}}_{n} not contained in 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D being D¯\overline{D}, SnS_{n}, FnF_{n}, and since SnS_{n} and FnF_{n} are smooth, the image of CC is D¯\overline{D}. Lemma 2.7 then shows that φ\varphi extends to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. ∎

Another direct corollary of Proposition 2.17 is the following (Corollary 2.19), which gives in particular a simple proof of the characterisation of birational endomorphisms of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} that contract only one irreducible curve, given by Daigle in [Dai91, Theorem 4.11].

Corollary 2.19.

Let C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be a geometrically irreducible closed curve and let φ:𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be an open embedding. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (i)(i)

    The extension of φ\varphi to a birational self-map of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} contracts the curve CC onto a point of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

  2. (i​i)(ii)

    The map φ\varphi extends to a birational endomorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, which is not an automorphism.

  3. (i​i​i)(iii)

    There exists automorphisms α,β\alpha,\beta of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} such that φ\varphi extends to the birational endomorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} given by α​ψ​β\alpha\psi\beta, where ψ:𝔸2→𝔸2\psi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2} is given by (x,y)↦(x,xn​y)(x,y)\mapsto(x,x^{n}y), for some integer n≥1n\geq 1.

In particular, if the assertions are satisfied ((or equivalently one of the assertions)), then C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} is equivalent to a line by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} and φ⁡(𝔸2∖C)=𝔸2∖D\varphi({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)={\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D, where DD is again a curve equivalent to a line by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

Proof.

(iii)⇒\Rightarrow(ii): follows from the fact that, for each n≥1n\geq 1, the map ψ:(x,y)↦(x,xn​y)\psi\colon(x,y)\mapsto(x,x^{n}y) is a birational endomorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} which is not an automorphism, as its inverse ψ−1:(x,y)↦(x,x−n​y)\psi^{-1}\colon(x,y)\mapsto(x,x^{-n}y) is not regular.

(ii)⇒\Rightarrow(i): Since φ\varphi extends to an endomorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} which is not an automorphism, the cases (1)-(2) of Lemma 2.7 are not possible. Hence, we are in case (3): CC is contracted onto a point of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, which is necessarily in 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} since φ⁡(𝔸2)⊂𝔸2\varphi({\mathbb{A}}^{2})\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

(i)⇒\Rightarrow(iii). By Lemma 2.7, φ⁡(𝔸2∖C)=𝔸2∖D\varphi({\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C)={\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D for some geometrically irreducible curve DD. Since CC is contracted onto a point of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, it is not possible to find an open embedding ι:𝔸2↪𝔽n\iota\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{F}}_{n}, for some n≥1n\geq 1, such that the rational map ι∘φ−1\iota\circ\varphi^{-1} extends to a regular morphism 𝔸2→𝔽n{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{F}}_{n}. By Proposition 2.17, this implies that DD is equivalent to a line by automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. Hence, the same holds for CC, by Lemma 2.13. Applying automorphisms of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} at the source and the target, we can then assume that C=DC=D is the line x=0x=0 and that φ\varphi extends to an endomorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} that contracts CC onto the origin. By Lemma 2.13(1), the map φ\varphi is of the form (x,y)↦(λ​x,μ​xn​y+s⁡(x))(x,y)\mapsto(\lambda x,\mu x^{n}y+s(x)), where λ,μ∈k∗\lambda,\mu\in\mathrm{k}^{*}, n≥1n\geq 1 and s∈k⁡[x]s\in\mathrm{k}[x] is a polynomial that vanishes at the origin. We then observe that φ\varphi is the composition of the automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} given by (λ​x,μ​y+s⁡(x​λ−1))(\lambda x,\mu y+s(x\lambda^{-1})) with (x,y)↦(x,xn​y)(x,y)\mapsto(x,x^{n}y) . ∎

2.5. Completion with two curves and a boundary

The following technical lemma (Lemma 2.22) is used to prove Corollary 2.23 and Proposition 2.25, which yield almost all statements of Theorem 1.

Definition 2.20.

Let XX be a smooth projective surface. A reduced closed curve C⊂XC\subset X is a k\mathrm{k}-forest of XX if CC is a finite union of closed curves C1,…,CnC_{1},\dots,C_{n}, all k\mathrm{k}-isomorphic to ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} and if each singular point of CC is a k\mathrm{k}-point lying on exactly two components Ci,CjC_{i},C_{j} intersecting transversally. We moreover ask that CC does not contain any loop. If CC is connected, we say that CC is a k\mathrm{k}-tree.

Remark 2.21.

If η:X→Y\eta\colon X\to Y is a birational morphism between smooth projective surfaces such that all base-points of η−1\eta^{-1} are defined over k\mathrm{k}, then the exceptional curve of η\eta (union of curves contracted) is a k\mathrm{k}-forest E⊂XE\subset X. Moreover, the strict transform and the preimage of any k\mathrm{k}-forest of YY is a k\mathrm{k}-forest of XX. The preimage of a k\mathrm{k}-tree is a k\mathrm{k}-tree.

Lemma 2.22.

Let C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be geometrically irreducible closed curves, not equivalent to lines by automorphisms of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} and let φ:𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D be an isomorphism which does not extend to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. Then, there is a smooth projective surface XX and two open embeddings ρ1,ρ2:𝔸2↪X\rho_{1},\rho_{2}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\hookrightarrow X such that ρ2​φ=ρ1\rho_{2}\varphi=\rho_{1} and such that the following holds:

  1. (i)(i)

    The curves Γ=ρ1​(C)¯⊂X\Gamma=\overline{\rho_{1}(C)}\subset X, Δ=ρ2​(D)¯⊂X\Delta=\overline{\rho_{2}(D)}\subset X are isomorphic to ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}.

  2. (i​i)(ii)

    For i=1,2i=1,2, we have ρi​(𝔸2)=X∖Bi\rho_{i}({\mathbb{A}}^{2})=X\setminus B_{i} for some k\mathrm{k}-tree BiB_{i}.

  3. (i​i​i)(iii)

    Writing B=B1∩B2B=B_{1}\cap B_{2}, we have B1=B∪ΔB_{1}=B\cup\Delta and B2=B∪ΓB_{2}=B\cup\Gamma.

  4. (i​v)(iv)

    There is no birational morphism X→YX\to Y, where YY is a smooth projective surface, which contracts one component of BB, and no other k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-curve.

  5. (v)(v)

    The number of connected components of BB is equal to the number of points of B∩ΓB\cap\Gamma and to the number of points of B∩ΔB\cap\Delta, and is at most 22.

Proof.

By Proposition 2.17, there exist integers m,n≥1m,n\geq 1, and isomorphisms

ι1:𝔸2⟶≃𝔽m∖(Sm∪Fm),ι2:𝔸2⟶≃𝔽n∖(Sn∪Fn)\iota_{1}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{F}}_{m}\setminus(S_{m}\cup F_{m}),\iota_{2}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{F}}_{n}\setminus(S_{n}\cup F_{n})

such that both open embeddings ι1​φ−1:𝔸2∖D→𝔽m\iota_{1}\varphi^{-1}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D\to{\mathbb{F}}_{m} and ι2​φ:𝔸2∖C→𝔽n\iota_{2}\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\to{\mathbb{F}}_{n} extend to regular morphisms u1:𝔸2→𝔽mu_{1}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{F}}_{m}, u2:𝔸2→𝔽nu_{2}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{F}}_{n}. Denoting by ψ:𝔽m⇢𝔽n\psi\colon{\mathbb{F}}_{m}\dasharrow{\mathbb{F}}_{n} the corresponding birational map, equal to ι2​(u1)−1=u2​(ι1)−1\iota_{2}(u_{1})^{-1}=u_{2}(\iota_{1})^{-1}, and taking a minimal resolution of the indeterminacies of ψ\psi, we get the following commutative diagram

where η\eta and π\pi are birational morphisms, which are sequences of blow-ups of k\mathrm{k}-points, being the base-points of ψ\psi and ψ−1\psi^{-1} respectively (the fact that all points are defined over k\mathrm{k} is because the curves contracted by ψ\psi and ψ−1\psi^{-1} are all geometrically irreducible k\mathrm{k}-curves, since they are contained in Sn,Fn,Sm,FnS_{n},F_{n},S_{m},F_{n} or the images of CC and DD and follows then from Lemma 2.6). Since u1,u2u_{1},u_{2} are regular on 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, the base-points of ψ\psi, resp. ψ−1\psi^{-1}, belong to Fm∪Sm⊂𝔽mF_{m}\cup S_{m}\subset{\mathbb{F}}_{m}, resp. Fn∪Sn⊂𝔽nF_{n}\cup S_{n}\subset{\mathbb{F}}_{n}. In particular, we get two open embeddings

ρ1=η−1​ι1:𝔸2↪X,ρ2=π−1​ι2:𝔸2↪X\rho_{1}=\eta^{-1}\iota_{1}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\hookrightarrow X,\rho_{2}=\pi^{-1}\iota_{2}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\hookrightarrow X

such that ρ2​φ=ρ1\rho_{2}\varphi=\rho_{1} (or more precisely ρ2​φ=ρ1|𝔸2∖C\rho_{2}\varphi=\rho_{1}|_{{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C}). We have ρ1​(𝔸2)=X∖B1\rho_{1}({\mathbb{A}}^{2})=X\setminus B_{1} and ρ2​(𝔸2)=X∖B2\rho_{2}({\mathbb{A}}^{2})=X\setminus B_{2}, where B1=η−1​(Sm∪Fm)B_{1}=\eta^{-1}(S_{m}\cup F_{m}) and B2=π−1​(Sn∪Fn)B_{2}=\pi^{-1}(S_{n}\cup F_{n}) are k\mathrm{k}-trees (see Remark 2.21). The fact that φ\varphi does not extend to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} implies that B1≠B2B_{1}\not=B_{2}. We then write B=B1∩B2B=B_{1}\cap B_{2} and observe that η⁡(B2∖B)\eta(B_{2}\setminus B) is a closed curve of 𝔽m∖η⁡(B)=ι1​(𝔸2){\mathbb{F}}_{m}\setminus\eta(B)=\iota_{1}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}), sent by ψ\psi outside of ι2​(𝔸2)\iota_{2}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}). This shows that C=η⁡(B2∖B)C=\eta(B_{2}\setminus B), and analogously one obtains D=π⁡(B1∖B)D=\pi(B_{1}\setminus B). Writing

Γ=ρ1​(C)¯⊂X,Δ=ρ2​(D)¯⊂X\Gamma=\overline{\rho_{1}(C)}\subset X,\Delta=\overline{\rho_{2}(D)}\subset X

we then obtain B2=B∪ΓB_{2}=B\cup\Gamma and B1=B∪ΔB_{1}=B\cup\Delta. In particular, since B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} are two k\mathrm{k}-trees, Γ\Gamma and Δ\Delta are isomorphic to ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} (over k\mathrm{k}) and intersect transversally BB in a finite number of k\mathrm{k}-points. Moreover, the number of connected components of BB is equal to the number of points of B∩ΓB\cap\Gamma, and of B∩ΔB\cap\Delta (which are all k\mathrm{k}-points as said before).

We have then found the surface XX together with the embeddings ι1,ι2\iota_{1},\iota_{2}, satisfying conditions (i)–(ii)–(iii). We will then modify XX if needed, in order to also get (iv)–(v).

Suppose that the number of connected components of BB is r≥3r\geq 3, and let us show that at least r−2r-2 connected components of BB are contractible (in the sense that there is a birational morphism X→YX\to Y, where YY is a smooth projective rational surface, which contracts one component of BB and no other k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-curve). To show this, we first observe that Γ\Gamma intersects rr distinct curves of BB. Since Γ\Gamma is one of the irreducible components of B2=π−1​(Sn∪Fn)B_{2}=\pi^{-1}(S_{n}\cup F_{n}), we can decompose π\pi as π2∘π1\pi_{2}\circ\pi_{1} where π1​(Γ)\pi_{1}(\Gamma) is an irreducible component of (π2)−1​(Sn∪Fn)(\pi_{2})^{-1}(S_{n}\cup F_{n}) intersecting exactly two other irreducible components R1,R2R_{1},R_{2}, and such that all points blown up by π1\pi_{1} are infinitely near points of π1​(Γ)∖(R1∪R2)\pi_{1}(\Gamma)\setminus(R_{1}\cup R_{2}). This proves that we can contract at least r−2r-2 connected components of BB.

If one connected component of BB is contractible, there exists a morphism X→YX\to Y, where YY is a smooth projective rational surface, which contracts this component of BB, and no other curve. Since the component intersects Δ\Delta transversally in one point, and also Γ\Gamma in one point, we can replace XX with YY, ι1,ι2\iota_{1},\iota_{2} with the composition with the morphism X→YX\to Y and still have conditions (i)–(ii)–(iii). After finitely many steps, condition (iv)(\ref{It4}) is satisfied. By the observation before, the number of connected components of BB, after this being done, is at most 22, giving then (v). ∎

Corollary 2.23.

Let C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be geometrically irreducible closed curves and let φ:𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D be an isomorphism which does not extend to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

Then, the curves C,DC,D are isomorphic to open subsets of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}: there exist polynomials P,Q∈k⁡[t]P,Q\in\mathrm{k}[t] without square factors, such that C≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])C\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}]) and D≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1Q])D\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}]). Moreover, the number of k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-roots of PP and QQ is the same ((i.e. extending the scalars to k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}, the curves CC and DD become isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} minus some finite number of points, the same number for both curves)). The number of k\mathrm{k}-roots of PP and QQ are also the same.

Remark 2.24.

When k=ℂ\mathrm{k}={\mathbb{C}}, this follows from the fact that CC and DD are isomorphic to open subsets of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, which is given by the fact that the curves are rational (Corollary 2.8) and smooth (Corollary 2.18). Indeed, since 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C and 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D are isomorphic, they have the same Euler characteristic, so CC and DD also have the same Euler characteristic.

Proof.

If CC or DD is equivalent to a line, so are both curves (Lemma 2.13), and the result holds. Otherwise, we apply Lemma 2.22 and get a smooth projective surface XX and two open embeddings ρ1,ρ2:𝔸2↪X\rho_{1},\rho_{2}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\hookrightarrow X such that ρ2​φ=ρ1\rho_{2}\varphi=\rho_{1} and satisfying the conditions (i)-(ii)-(iii)-(iv)-(v). In particular, CC is isomorphic to Γ∖B1=Γ∖((Γ∩B)∪(Γ∪Δ))\Gamma\setminus B_{1}=\Gamma\setminus((\Gamma\cap B)\cup(\Gamma\cup\Delta)). Since Γ\Gamma is isomorphic to ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} and Γ∩B\Gamma\cap B consists of one or two k\mathrm{k}-points, this shows that Γ\Gamma is isomorphic to an open subset of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. Doing the same for DD, we get isomorphisms C≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])C\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}]) and D≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1Q])D\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}]) where P,Q∈k⁡[t]P,Q\in\mathrm{k}[t] are polynomials, that we can assume without square factors.

The number of k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-roots of PP is equal to the number of k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-points of Γ∩B1\Gamma\cap B_{1} plus 11. Similarly, the number of k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-roots of QQ is equal to the number of k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-points of Δ∩B2\Delta\cap B_{2} plus 11. To see that these numbers are equal, we observe that Γ∩B1=(Γ∩B)∪(Γ∩Δ)\Gamma\cap B_{1}=(\Gamma\cap B)\cup(\Gamma\cap\Delta), that Δ∩B2=(Δ∩B)∪(Δ∩Γ)\Delta\cap B_{2}=(\Delta\cap B)\cup(\Delta\cap\Gamma), and that the number of points of Γ∩B\Gamma\cap B is the same as the number of points of Δ∩B\Delta\cap B (follows from (v)). As each point of Γ∩B\Gamma\cap B that is also contained in Γ∩Δ\Gamma\cap\Delta is also contained in Δ∩B\Delta\cap B, this shows that PP and QQ have the same number of k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-roots. As each k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-point of Γ∩B1\Gamma\cap B_{1} or Δ∩B2\Delta\cap B_{2} which is not a k\mathrm{k}-point is contained in Γ∩Δ\Gamma\cap\Delta, the number of k\mathrm{k}-roots of PP and QQ is also the same.∎

Proposition 2.25.

Let C,D,D′⊂𝔸2C,D,D^{\prime}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be geometrically irreducible closed curves, not equivalent to lines by automorphisms of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, and let φ:𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D, φ′:𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D′\varphi^{\prime}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D^{\prime} be isomorphisms which do not extend to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. Then, one of the following holds:

  1. (a)(a)

    The map φ′​(φ)−1\varphi^{\prime}(\varphi)^{-1} extends to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} ((sending DD to OPEND′)D^{\prime});

  2. (b)(b)

    The three curves C,D,D′C,D,D^{\prime} are k\mathrm{k}-isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1};

  3. (c)(c)

    The three curves C,D,D′C,D,D^{\prime} are k\mathrm{k}-isomorphic to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}.

Remark 2.26.

Case (b) never happens, as we will show after. Indeed, since CC is not equivalent to a line, the existence of φ,φ′\varphi,\varphi^{\prime} is prohibited (Proposition 2.28 below).

Proof.

If C≃𝔸1C\simeq{\mathbb{A}}^{1} or C≃𝔸1∖{0}C\simeq{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}, then D≃C≃D′D\simeq C\simeq D^{\prime} by Corollary 2.23. We can thus assume that CC is not isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} or 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}. We apply Lemma 2.22 with φ\varphi and φ′\varphi^{\prime} and get smooth projective surfaces X,X′X,X^{\prime} and open embeddings ρ1,ρ2,ρ1′,ρ2′:𝔸2↪X\rho_{1},\rho_{2},\rho_{1}^{\prime},\rho_{2}^{\prime}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\hookrightarrow X such that ρ2​φ=ρ1\rho_{2}\varphi=\rho_{1}, ρ2′​φ′=ρ1′\rho_{2}^{\prime}\varphi^{\prime}=\rho_{1}^{\prime} and satisfying the conditions (i)-(ii)-(iii)-(iv)-(v). In particular, we obtain an isomorphism κ:X∖(B∪Γ∪Δ)⟶≃X′∖(B′∪Γ′∪Δ′)\kappa\colon X\setminus(B\cup\Gamma\cup\Delta)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}X^{\prime}\setminus(B^{\prime}\cup\Gamma^{\prime}\cup\Delta^{\prime}) (where Γ=ρ1​(C)¯⊂X\Gamma=\overline{\rho_{1}(C)}\subset X, Δ=ρ2​(D)¯⊂X\Delta=\overline{\rho_{2}(D)}\subset X, Γ′=ρ1′​(C)¯⊂X′\Gamma^{\prime}=\overline{\rho_{1}^{\prime}(C)}\subset X^{\prime}, Δ′=ρ2′​(D′)¯⊂X′\Delta^{\prime}=\overline{\rho_{2}^{\prime}(D^{\prime})}\subset X^{\prime}) and a commutative diagram

By construction, κ\kappa sends birationally Γ=ρ1​(C)¯\Gamma=\overline{\rho_{1}(C)} onto Γ′=ρ1′​(C)¯\Gamma^{\prime}=\overline{\rho_{1}^{\prime}(C)}. 2.6. The case of curves isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} and the proof of Theorem 1

To finish the proof of Theorem 1, one still needs to do the case of curves isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. The case of lines has been already treated in Lemma 2.13. In characteristic zero, this finishes the study by the Abyhankar-Moh-Suzuki theorem, but in positive characteristic, there are many closed curves of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} which are isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} but are not equivalent to lines (these curves are sometimes called “bad lines” in the literature). We will show that an open embedding 𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} always extends to 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} if CC is isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} but not equivalent to a line.

Lemma 2.27.

Let n≥1n\geq 1 and let Γ⊂𝔽n\Gamma\subset{\mathbb{F}}_{n} be a closed geometrically irreducible curve, such that Γ⋅Fn≥2\Gamma\cdot F_{n}\geq 2.
