Proposition 2.28.

Let C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be a closed curve, isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} ((i.e. isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} over 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁k)\mathrm{k}). The following are equivalent:

  1. (a)(a)

    The curve CC is equivalent to a line by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

  2. (b)(b)

    There exists an open embedding 𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} which does not extend to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

  3. (c)(c)

    Embedding 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} into ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, via the canonical embedding, there exists a birational map of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} that contracts the curve CC onto a point ((and maybe contracts other curves)).

Proof.

The implications (a)⇒(b)(\ref{1Ceqline})\Rightarrow(\ref{2contractA2}) and (a)⇒(c)(\ref{1Ceqline})\Rightarrow(\ref{3contractP2}) can be observed, for example by taking the map (x,y)↦(x,x​y)(x,y)\mapsto(x,xy), which is an open embedding of 𝔸2∖{x=0}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus\{x=0\} into 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, which does not extend to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, and whose extension to ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} contracts the line x=0x=0 onto a point.

To prove (b)⇒(c)(\ref{2contractA2})\Rightarrow(\ref{3contractP2}), we take an open embedding φ:𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} which does not extend to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} and look at the extension to ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}. By Lemma 2.7, either this one contracts CC, or CC is equivalent to a line, in which case (c)(\ref{3contractP2}) is true as was shown before.

It remains to prove (c)⇒(a)(\ref{3contractP2})\Rightarrow(\ref{1Ceqline}). We apply Lemma 2.16, and obtain an isomorphism ι:𝔸2⟶≃𝔽n\(Sn∪Fn)\iota\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{F}}_{n}\backslash(S_{n}\cup F_{n}) such that the closure of ι⁡(C)\iota(C) in 𝔽n{\mathbb{F}}_{n} is a curve Γ\Gamma which satisfies one of the two cases (1)(\ref{SectionCase})-(2)(\ref{ng}) of Lemma 2.16. In case (1)(\ref{SectionCase}), the curve is equivalent to a line as it is isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} (equivalence (ii)−(iiiCLOSE(\ref{LL2})-(\ref{LL3}) of Lemma 2.16). It remains to study the case where Γ\Gamma satisfies the conditions (2)(\ref{ng}) of Lemma 2.16 (in particular Γ⋅Fn≥2\Gamma\cdot F_{n}\geq 2), and to show that these, together with (c)(\ref{3contractP2}), yield a contradiction. We prove that there is no point p∈𝔽n​(k¯)p\in{\mathbb{F}}_{n}(\overline{\mathrm{k}}) such that 2​mp​(Γ)>Γ⋅Fn2m_{p}(\Gamma)>\Gamma\cdot F_{n}. Indeed, since Γ⋅Fn≥2\Gamma\cdot F_{n}\geq 2, the point would be a singular point of Γ\Gamma, and since Γ∖(Fn∪En)=C\Gamma\setminus(F_{n}\cup E_{n})=C is isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, pp is a k\mathrm{k}-point and is the unique k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-point of Γ∩(Fn∪En)\Gamma\cap(F_{n}\cup E_{n}). Moreover, as Γ⋅Fn≥2\Gamma\cdot F_{n}\geq 2, we find that p∈Fnp\in F_{n}. Since 2​mp​(Γ)>Γ⋅Fn2m_{p}(\Gamma)>\Gamma\cdot F_{n} and because Γ\Gamma satisfies the conditions (2) of Lemma 2.16, the only possibility is that n=1n=1, p∈F1∖S1p\in F_{1}\setminus S_{1} and 0<mp​(Γ)≤Γ⋅S10<m_{p}(\Gamma)\leq\Gamma\cdot S_{1}. This is impossible as it contradicts the fact that Γ∩(S1∪F1)\Gamma\cap(S_{1}\cup F_{1}) contains only one k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-point.

Denote by ψ0:ℙ2⇢ℙ2\psi_{0}\colon{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2} the birational map that contracts CC (and maybe other curves) onto a point. Observe that ψ0∘ι−1\psi_{0}\circ\iota^{-1} yields a birational map ψ:𝔽n⇢ℙ2\psi\colon{\mathbb{F}}_{n}\dasharrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2} which contracts Γ\Gamma onto a point. As there is no point p∈𝔽n​(k¯)p\in{\mathbb{F}}_{n}(\overline{\mathrm{k}}) such that 2​mp​(Γ)>Γ⋅Fn2m_{p}(\Gamma)>\Gamma\cdot F_{n}, Lemma 2.27 implies that n=1n=1 and that there exists a point p∈𝔽1​(k¯)∖S1p\in{\mathbb{F}}_{1}(\overline{\mathrm{k}})\setminus S_{1} such that mp​(Γ)>Γ⋅S1m_{p}(\Gamma)>\Gamma\cdot S_{1}. Again, this point is a k\mathrm{k}-point, since CC is k\mathrm{k}-isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. This contradicts the conditions (2)(\ref{ng}) of Lemma 2.16. ∎

Remark 2.29.

If the field k\mathrm{k} is perfect, then every curve that is geometrically isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} (i.e. over k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}) is also isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. This can be seen by embedding the curve in ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} and looking at the complement point, necessarily defined over k\mathrm{k}. For non-perfect fields, there exist closed curves C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} geometrically isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} but not isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} (see [Rus70]). Corollary 2.23 shows that every open embedding 𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} extends to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} for all such curves.

We can now finish the section by proving Theorem 1:

Proof of Theorem 1.

We recall the hypothesis of the theorem: we have a geometrically irreducible closed curve C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} and an isomorphism φ:𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D for some closed curve C⊂𝔸2C\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. Assume that φ\varphi does not extend to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

(1): If CC is isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, then Proposition 2.28(a) shows that CC is equivalent to a line and Lemma 2.13(2) implies that the same holds for DD. In particular, the curves CC and DD are isomorphic.

If CC is isomorphic to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\} then so is DD by Corollary 2.23.

(2): if CC is not isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} or to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}, then Proposition 2.25 shows that the isomorphism φ:𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D\varphi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D (not extending to an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}) is uniquely determined by CC, up to post-composition by an automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. In particular, there are at most two equivalence classes of curves of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} having complements isomorphic to 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C. Corollary 2.23 achieves the proof by giving the existence of isomorphisms C≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])C\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}]) and D≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1Q])D\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}]) for some polynomials P,Q∈k⁡[t]P,Q\in\mathrm{k}[t] without square factors having the same number of roots in k\mathrm{k}, and having also the same number of roots in the algebraic closure of k\mathrm{k}. ∎

3. Families of different embeddings given by sections of line bundles

3.1. A construction using elements of SL2⁡(k⁡[y])\SL_{2}(\mathrm{k}[y])

As we observed in Lemma 2.16 and its applications, the curves of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} given by

a⁡(y)​x+b⁡(y)=0a(y)x+b(y)=0

for some coprime polynomials a,b∈k⁡[y]a,b\in\mathrm{k}[y], a≠0a\not=0 (where we can always assume that deg⁡b<deg⁡a\deg b<\deg a), yield a natural family which plays an important role. We study this family here. Recall that such curves are equivalent to a line if and only a⁡(y)a(y) is a constant (Lemma 2.16(i)-(ii)), which is a case already treated in Lemma 2.13. We can thus assume that deg⁡(a)≥1\deg(a)\geq 1, and thus that deg⁡(b)≥0\deg(b)\geq 0 (i.e. that b≠0b\not=0) since the polynomial a⁡(y)​x+b⁡(y)a(y)x+b(y) has to be irreducible.

Lemma 3.1.

For each matrix (a⁡(y)b⁡(y)c⁡(y)d⁡(y))∈SL2⁡(k⁡[y])\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}a(y)&b(y)\\ c(y)&d(y)\end{array}\right)\in\SL_{2}(\mathrm{k}[y]), we have an isomorphism

φ:𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D(x,y)↦(c⁡(y)​x+d⁡(y)a⁡(y)​x+b⁡(y),y)\begin{array}[]{rrcl}\varphi\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D\\ &(x,y)&\mapsto&\big(\frac{c(y)x+d(y)}{a(y)x+b(y)},y\big)\end{array}

where C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} are given by a⁡(y)​x+b⁡(y)=0a(y)x+b(y)=0 and a⁡(y)​x−c⁡(y)=0a(y)x-c(y)=0 respectively.

Proof.

Note first that φ\varphi is a birational transformation of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, with inverse ψ:(x,y)↦(−b⁡(y)​x+d⁡(y)a⁡(y)​x−c⁡(y),y)\psi\colon(x,y)\mapsto(\frac{-b(y)x+d(y)}{a(y)x-c(y)},y). It remains to prove that the isomorphism φ∗:k⁡(x,y)→k⁡(x,y)\varphi^{*}\colon\mathrm{k}(x,y)\to\mathrm{k}(x,y), x↦c​x+da​x+bx\mapsto\frac{cx+d}{ax+b}, y↦yy\mapsto y induces an isomorphism k⁡[x,y,1a​x−c]→k⁡[x,y,1a​x+b].\mathrm{k}[x,y,\frac{1}{ax-c}]\to\mathrm{k}[x,y,\frac{1}{ax+b}]. This follows from

φ∗​({x,y,1a​x−c})={c​x+da​x+b,y,a​x+b}\varphi^{*}(\{x,y,\frac{1}{ax-c}\})=\{\frac{cx+d}{ax+b},y,ax+b\} and ψ∗​({x,y,1a​x+b})={−b​x+da​x−c,y,a​x−b}.\psi^{*}(\{x,y,\frac{1}{ax+b}\})=\{\frac{-bx+d}{ax-c},y,ax-b\}. ∎

The curves CC and DD of Lemma 3.1 are always isomorphic, but are in general not equivalent, as we now prove.

Lemma 3.2.

Let C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be two irreducible curves given by

a⁡(y)​x+b⁡(y)=0​ and ​a~​(y)​x+b~​(y)=0a(y)x+b(y)=0\mbox{ and }\tilde{a}(y)x+\tilde{b}(y)=0

respectively, for some a,b,a~,b~∈k⁡[y]a,b,\tilde{a},\tilde{b}\in\mathrm{k}[y], such that deg⁡(a)>deg⁡(b)≥0\deg(a)>\deg(b)\geq 0 and deg⁡(a~)>deg⁡(b~)≥0\deg(\tilde{a})>\deg(\tilde{b})\geq 0.

  1. (1)(1)

    The curves CC and DD are isomorphic to Spec⁡(k⁡[y,1a])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[y,\frac{1}{a}]) and Spec⁡(k⁡[y,1a~])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[y,\frac{1}{\tilde{a}}]) respectively.

  2. (2)(2)

    The curves CC and DD are equivalent if and only if there exist α,λ,μ∈k∗\alpha,\lambda,\mu\in\mathrm{k}^{*}, β∈k\beta\in\mathrm{k} such that

    a~​(y)=λ⋅a⁡(α​y+β),b~​(y)=μ⋅b⁡(α​y+β).\tilde{a}(y)=\lambda\cdot a(\alpha y+\beta),\quad\tilde{b}(y)=\mu\cdot b(\alpha y+\beta).
Proof.

The proof of (1) is given by

k[C]=k[x,y]/(a(y)x+b(y))≃k[y,−b(y)/a(y)]=k[y,1/a(y)],\mathrm{k}[C]=\mathrm{k}[x,y]/(a(y)x+b(y))\simeq\mathrm{k}[y,-b(y)/a(y)]=\mathrm{k}[y,1/a(y)],

where the last equality comes from the fact that a,b∈k⁡[y]a,b\in\mathrm{k}[y] are coprime (since CC is irreducible), so there exist c,d∈k⁡[y]c,d\in\mathrm{k}[y] with a​d−b​c=1ad-bc=1, which implies that 1a=a​d−b​ca=d−c⋅ba∈k⁡[y,ba]\frac{1}{a}=\frac{ad-bc}{a}=d-c\cdot\frac{b}{a}\in\mathrm{k}[y,\frac{b}{a}]. The isomorphism D≃Spec⁡(k⁡[y,1a~])D\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[y,\frac{1}{\tilde{a}}]) is analogous.

To prove (2), we first observe that if a~​(y)=λ⋅a⁡(α​y+β)\tilde{a}(y)=\lambda\cdot a(\alpha y+\beta) and b~​(y)=μ⋅b⁡(α​y+β)\tilde{b}(y)=\mu\cdot b(\alpha y+\beta) for some α,λ,μ∈k∗\alpha,\lambda,\mu\in\mathrm{k}^{*}, β∈k\beta\in\mathrm{k}, then the automorphism (x,y)↦(λμ​x,α​y+β)(x,y)\mapsto(\frac{\lambda}{\mu}x,\alpha y+\beta) of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} sends DD to CC.

Conversely, we assume the existence of φ∈Aut⁡(𝔸2)\varphi\in\Aut({\mathbb{A}}^{2}) that sends DD onto CC and want to find α,λ,μ∈k∗\alpha,\lambda,\mu\in\mathrm{k}^{*}, β∈k\beta\in\mathrm{k} as above. Writing φ\varphi as (x,y)↦(f⁡(x,y),g⁡(x,y))(x,y)\mapsto(f(x,y),g(x,y)) for some f,g∈k⁡[x,y]f,g\in\mathrm{k}[x,y], one gets

(A) μ⁡(a⁡(g)​f+b⁡(g))=a~​x+b~\mu(a(g)f+b(g))=\tilde{a}x+\tilde{b}

for some μ∈k∗\mu\in\mathrm{k}^{*}.

(i)(i) If g∈k⁡[y]g\in\mathrm{k}[y], the fact that k⁡[f,g]=k⁡[x,y]\mathrm{k}[f,g]=\mathrm{k}[x,y] implies that g=α​y+β,f=γ​x+sg=\alpha y+\beta,f=\gamma x+s for some α,γ∈k∗,β∈k,s∈k⁡[y]\alpha,\gamma\in\mathrm{k}^{*},\beta\in\mathrm{k},s\in\mathrm{k}[y], and yields a⁡(g)​f+b⁡(g)=a⁡(g)​(γ​x+s)+b⁡(g)a(g)f+b(g)=a(g)(\gamma x+s)+b(g), so Equation (A) yields:

a~=μ​γ⋅a⁡(g),b~=μ⋅(a⁡(g)​s+b⁡(g)).\tilde{a}=\mu\gamma\cdot a(g),\ \tilde{b}=\mu\cdot(a(g)s+b(g)).

This shows in particular that deg⁡a=deg⁡a~\deg a=\deg\tilde{a}, whence deg⁡b~<deg⁡a⁡(g)\deg\tilde{b}<\deg a(g). Since deg⁡(b⁡(g))<deg⁡a⁡(g)\deg(b(g))<\deg a(g), we find that s=0s=0, and thus that b~=μ⋅b⁡(g)\tilde{b}=\mu\cdot b(g), as desired. This ends the proof, by choosing λ=μ​γ\lambda=\mu\gamma.

(i​i)(ii) It remains to study the case where g∉k⁡[y]g\notin\mathrm{k}[y], which corresponds to degx⁡(g)≥1\deg_{x}(g)\geq 1 and yields degx⁡(a⁡(g))=deg⁡(a)⋅degx⁡(g)>deg⁡(b)⋅degx⁡(g)=degx⁡(b⁡(g))\deg_{x}(a(g))=\deg(a)\cdot\deg_{x}(g)>\deg(b)\cdot\deg_{x}(g)=\deg_{x}(b(g)), which implies that degx⁡(a⁡(g)​f+b⁡(g))=deg⁡(a)⋅degx⁡(g)+degx⁡(f)\deg_{x}(a(g)f+b(g))=\deg(a)\cdot\deg_{x}(g)+\deg_{x}(f). Equation (A) shows that this degree is 11, and since deg⁡(a)≥1\deg(a)\geq 1, we find deg⁡(a)=1\deg(a)=1. Similarly, the automorphism sending CC to DD satisfies the same condition, so deg⁡(a~)=1\deg(\tilde{a})=1. This implies that b,b~∈k∗b,\tilde{b}\in\mathrm{k}^{*}. There exist thus some α,λ,μ∈k∗\alpha,\lambda,\mu\in\mathrm{k}^{*}, β∈k\beta\in\mathrm{k} such that a~​(y)=λ⋅a⁡(α​y+β),b~​(y)=μ⋅b⁡(α​y+β)\tilde{a}(y)=\lambda\cdot a(\alpha y+\beta),\tilde{b}(y)=\mu\cdot b(\alpha y+\beta). ∎

Corollary 3.3.

For each polynomial f∈k⁡[t]f\in\mathrm{k}[t] of degree ≥1\geq 1, there exist two closed curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} both isomorphic to Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1f])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{f}]), but not equivalent, such that 𝔸2∖C≃𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\simeq{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D. Moreover, the set of such pairs of closed embeddings, up to equivalence, is infinite.

Proof.

We choose an irreducible polynomial b∈k⁡[t]b\in\mathrm{k}[t] which does not divide ff. We then choose, for each n≥1n\geq 1 such that deg⁡(fn)>2​deg⁡(b)\deg(f^{n})>2\deg(b), two polynomials c,d∈k⁡[t]c,d\in\mathrm{k}[t] such that fn​d−b​c=1f^{n}d-bc=1.

The curves Cn,Dn⊂𝔸2C_{n},D_{n}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} given by fn​x+b=0f^{n}x+b=0 and fn​x−c=0f^{n}x-c=0 are both isomorphic to Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1fn])=Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1f])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{f^{n}}])=\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{f}]) (Lemma 3.2(1)) and have isomorphic complements (Lemma 3.1). Moreover, as deg⁡b​c=deg⁡(fn​d−1)≥deg⁡(fn)>2​deg⁡(b)\deg bc=\deg(f^{n}d-1)\geq\deg(f^{n})>2\deg(b), we find that deg⁡c>deg⁡b\deg c>\deg b, which implies that CnC_{n} and DnD_{n} are not equivalent (Lemma 3.2(2)). Moreover, the curves CnC_{n} are all non-equivalent, again by Lemma 3.2(2). ∎

3.2. Curves isomorphic to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}

We consider now families of curves of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} of the form x​yd+y​P​(y)+1=0xy^{d}+yP(y)+1=0 for some d≥1d\geq 1 and some polynomial P∈k⁡[y]P\in\mathrm{k}[y] (which can be chosen to be of degree ≤d−2\leq d-2). Note that all these curves are isomorphic to Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1td])=Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1t])≃𝔸1∖{0}\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{t^{d}}])=\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{t}])\simeq{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\} (Lemma 3.2(1)).

Lemma 3.4.

Let d≥1d\geq 1 be an integer. For each polynomial P∈k⁡[y]P\in\mathrm{k}[y] of degree ≤d−2\leq d-2, one defines CP⊂𝔸2C_{P}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} to be the curve given by

x​yd+y​P​(y)+1=0.xy^{d}+yP(y)+1=0.
  1. (1)(1)

    Fixing some polynomial P∈k⁡[y]P\in\mathrm{k}[y] of degree ≤d−2\leq d-2, there exists, for each integer m≥1m\geq 1, a unique polynomial Q∈k⁡[y]Q\in\mathrm{k}[y] of degree ≤d−2\leq d-2 satisfying

    (B) P⁡(y)≡(y​P​(y)+1)m​Q​(y​(y​P​(y)+1)m)(modyd−1).P(y)\equiv(yP(y)+1)^{m}Q(y(yP(y)+1)^{m})\pmod{y^{d-1}}.

    There exist then fm∈k⁡[x,y]f_{m}\in\mathrm{k}[x,y] and λ∈k\lambda\in\mathrm{k} that give an isomorphism

    ψm:𝔸2∖CP⟶≃𝔸2∖CQ(x,y)↦(x+λ+y​fm​(x,y)(x​yd+y​P​(y)+1)m​d,y​(x​yd+y​P​(y)+1)m).\begin{array}[]{rccc}\psi_{m}\colon&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{P}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}&{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{Q}\\ &(x,y)&\mapsto&\left(\frac{x+\lambda+yf_{m}(x,y)}{(xy^{d}+yP(y)+1)^{md}},\,y(xy^{d}+yP(y)+1)^{m}\right).\end{array}
  2. (2)(2)

    For all integers m>m′≥1m>m^{\prime}\geq 1, the open embeddings ψm,ψm′:𝔸2∖CP↪𝔸2\psi_{m},\psi_{m^{\prime}}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{P}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} are not equal, up to automorphisms of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

Proof.

(1): We first observe that if d=1d=1, then (1) is trivially true, with P=Q=0P=Q=0 (these are the only polynomials of degree ≤d−2\leq d-2), by choosing fm=xf_{m}=x. Indeed, the map (x,y)↦(x(x​y+1)m,y​(x​y+1)m)(x,y)\mapsto\left(\frac{x}{(xy+1)^{m}},y(xy+1)^{m}\right) yields an automorphism of 𝔸2∖CP=𝔸2∖CQ{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{P}={\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{Q}, whose inverse is (x,y)↦(x​(x​y+1)m,y(x​y+1)m)(x,y)\mapsto\left(x(xy+1)^{m},\frac{y}{(xy+1)^{m}}\right). We then assume that d≥2d\geq 2.

For each polynomial R∈k⁡[x]R\in\mathrm{k}[x] of degree ≤d−2\leq d-2, one defines

φR:(x,y)↦(x​yd+y​R​(y)+1,y)\varphi_{R}\colon(x,y)\mapsto(xy^{d}+yR(y)+1,y)

which is a birational morphism ψR:𝔸2→𝔸2\psi_{R}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, that contracts the line Ly⊂𝔸2L_{y}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} given by y=0y=0 onto the point (1,0)(1,0), and induces an automorphism of 𝔸2∖Ly{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus L_{y}. Indeed, the inverse (φR)−1:𝔸2⇢𝔸2(\varphi_{R})^{-1}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2} is given by (φR)−1:(x,y)↦(x−y​R​(y)−1yd,y),(\varphi_{R})^{-1}\colon(x,y)\mapsto\left(\frac{x-yR(y)-1}{y^{d}},y\right), so (φR)∗∈Aut⁡(k⁡(x,y))(\varphi_{R})^{*}\in\Aut(\mathrm{k}(x,y)) restricts to an automorphism of k⁡[x,y,1y]\mathrm{k}[x,y,\frac{1}{y}].

We fix some P∈k⁡[x]P\in\mathrm{k}[x] of degree ≤d−2\leq d-2, choose some integer m≥1m\geq 1 and observe that (y​P​(y)+1)m(yP(y)+1)^{m} is invertible in k⁡[y]/(yd−1)\mathrm{k}[y]/(y^{d-1}) since y​P​(y)yP(y) is nilpotent. This shows that Equation (B) has a unique solution in k⁡[y]/(yd−1)\mathrm{k}[y]/(y^{d-1}), so we get a unique polynomial QQ of degree ≤d−2\leq d-2 satisfying it. We then consider the birational map

ψm=(φQ)−1​τ​φP\psi_{m}=(\varphi_{Q})^{-1}\tau\varphi_{P}

where τ:𝔸2→𝔸2\tau\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2} is the birational endomorphism given by (x,y)↦(x,xm​y)(x,y)\mapsto(x,x^{m}y) (that fixes the point (1,0)(1,0) and induces a local isomorphism around this point). The map ψm\psi_{m} is constructed so that it induces an isomorphism 𝔸2∖(Ly∪CP)⟶≃𝔸2∖(Ly∪CQ){\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus(L_{y}\cup C_{P})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus(L_{y}\cup C_{Q}) (this does not depend on the choice of QQ). It remains to see that the choice of QQ implies that ψm\psi_{m} extends to an isomorphism 𝔸2∖CP⟶≃𝔸2∖CQ{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{P}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{Q} of the desired form. Since QQ satisfies Equation (B), we find

(C) P⁡(y)≡(y​P​(y)+1)m​Q​(y​(y​P​(y)+1)m)+λ​yd−1(modyd)P(y)\equiv(yP(y)+1)^{m}Q(y(yP(y)+1)^{m})+\lambda y^{d-1}\pmod{y^{d}}

for some λ∈k\lambda\in\mathrm{k}. We then compute ψ⁡(x,y)\psi(x,y), and find

(x​yd+y⁡(P⁡(y)−(x​yd+y​P​(y)+1)m​Q​(y​(x​yd+y​P​(y)+1)m))yd​(x​yd+y​P​(y)+1)m​d,y​(x​yd+y​P​(y)+1)m)\left(\frac{xy^{d}+y\left(P(y)-(xy^{d}+yP(y)+1)^{m}Q(y(xy^{d}+yP(y)+1)^{m})\right)}{y^{d}(xy^{d}+yP(y)+1)^{md}},y(xy^{d}+yP(y)+1)^{m}\right)

which can be written, using Equation (C), as

ψ⁡(x,y)=(x+λ+y​fm​(x,y)(x​yd+y​P​(y)+1)m​d,y​(x​yd+y​P​(y)+1)m)\psi(x,y)=\left(\frac{x+\lambda+yf_{m}(x,y)}{(xy^{d}+yP(y)+1)^{md}},y(xy^{d}+yP(y)+1)^{m}\right)

for some polynomial fm∈k⁡[x,y]f_{m}\in\mathrm{k}[x,y]. This shows that ψm\psi_{m} restricts to the automorphism x↦x+λx\mapsto x+\lambda on LyL_{y} and then restricts to an isomorphism 𝔸2∖CP⟶≃𝔸2∖CQ{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{P}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{Q} of the desired form, achieving the proof of (1).

To prove (2), we observe that, since x+λ+y​fm​(x,y)≡x+λ(mody)x+\lambda+yf_{m}(x,y)\equiv x+\lambda\pmod{y}, the polynomial x+λ+y​fm​(x,y)x+\lambda+yf_{m}(x,y) is not divisible by x​yd+y​P​(y)+1xy^{d}+yP(y)+1. In particular, applying any automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} to ψm\psi_{m}, we cannot decrease the degree of the denominators, and thus do not get any ψm′\psi_{m^{\prime}}, for m′<mm^{\prime}<m. ∎

Remark 3.5.

Geometrically, the construction of Lemma 3.4 can be interpreted as follows: the birational morphism φP:(x,y)↦(x​yd+y​P​(y)+1,y)\varphi_{P}\colon(x,y)\mapsto(xy^{d}+yP(y)+1,y) contracts the line y=0y=0 onto the point (1,0)(1,0). If n=1n=1 then φP\varphi_{P} just sends the line onto the exceptional divisor of (1,0)(1,0). If n≥2n\geq 2, it sends the line onto the exceptional divisor of a point in the (n−1)(n-1)-th neighbourhood of (1,0)(1,0). The coordinates of these points are determined by PP. The fact that τ:(x,y)↦(x,xm​y)\tau\colon(x,y)\mapsto(x,x^{m}y) contracts x=0x=0 implies that ψm\psi_{m} contracts the curve x​yd+y​P​(y)+1=0xy^{d}+yP(y)+1=0. Moreover, τ\tau fixes the point (1,0)(1,0) and induces a local isomorphism around it, so acts on the set of infinitely near points. This action changes the polynomial PP and replaces it with another one, which is the polynomial QQ provided by Lemma 3.4.

Corollary 3.6.

For each field k\mathrm{k}, there exists an infinite sequence of curves Ci⊂𝔸2C_{i}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}, all pairwise not equivalent under automorphisms, all isomorphic to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\} and such that for each ii there are infinitely many open embeddings 𝔸2∖Ci↪𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{i}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, up to automorphisms of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

Proof.

It suffices to choose the curve CiC_{i} given by x​yi+2+y+1xy^{i+2}+y+1, for each i≥2i\geq 2. These curves are all isomorphic to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\} (Lemma 3.2(1)) and are pairwise not equivalent, under automorphisms of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} (Lemma 3.2(2)). The existence of infinitely many open embeddings 𝔸2∖C↪𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, up to automorphisms of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, is then provided by Lemma 3.4. ∎

One can compute the polynomial QQ provided by Lemma 3.4, in terms of PP, mm and dd, and find explicit formulas. We find in particular the following result:

Lemma 3.7.

For each μ∈k\mu\in\mathrm{k}, we denote by Cμ⊂𝔸2C_{\mu}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} the curve given by

x​y3+μ​y2+y+1=0.xy^{3}+\mu y^{2}+y+1=0.

Then, there exists an isomorphism 𝔸2∖Cμ→𝔸2∖Cμ−1{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{\mu}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{\mu-1}, for each μ∈k\mu\in\mathrm{k}. In particular, if char⁡(k)=0\mathrm{char}(\mathrm{k})=0, we obtain infinitely many closed curves of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, not equivalent under automorphism of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, which have isomorphic complements.

Proof.

To get the isomorphism 𝔸2∖Cμ→𝔸2∖Cμ−1{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{\mu}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{\mu-1}, it suffices to apply Lemma 3.4 with d=3d=3, P=μ​y+1P=\mu y+1, m=1m=1, and check that Q=(μ−1)​y+1Q=(\mu-1)y+1. One needs to see that

P⁡(y)≡(y​P​(y)+1)​Q​(y⁡(y​P​(y)+1))(mody2).P(y)\equiv(yP(y)+1)Q\big(y(yP(y)+1)\big)\pmod{y^{2}}.

(see Equation (B) in Lemma 3.4). Indeed, one finds, since y​P​(y)≡y(mody2)yP(y)\equiv y\pmod{y^{2}}, that

(y​P​(y)+1)​Q​(y⁡(y​P​(y)+1))≡(y+1)​Q​(y)≡Q⁡(y)+y≡P⁡(y)(mody2).\begin{array}[]{rcl}(yP(y)+1)Q\big(y(yP(y)+1)\big)\equiv(y+1)Q(y)\equiv Q(y)+y\equiv P(y)\pmod{y^{2}}.\end{array}

To get the last statement, one assumes that char⁡(k)=0\mathrm{char}(\mathrm{k})=0 and observes that the affine surfaces 𝔸2∖Cn{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{n} are all isomorphic for each n∈ℤn\in{\mathbb{Z}}. To show that the curves CnC_{n}, n∈ℤn\in{\mathbb{Z}} are pairwise non-equivalent, we apply Lemma 3.2(2): for m,n∈ℤm,n\in{\mathbb{Z}}, the curves CmC_{m} and CnC_{n} are equivalent only if there exist α,λ,μ∈k∗\alpha,\lambda,\mu\in\mathrm{k}^{*}, β∈k\beta\in\mathrm{k} such that

y3=λ⋅(α​y+β)3,m​y2+y+1=μ⋅(n​(α​y+β)2+(α​y+β)+1).y^{3}=\lambda\cdot(\alpha y+\beta)^{3},\ my^{2}+y+1=\mu\cdot(n(\alpha y+\beta)^{2}+(\alpha y+\beta)+1).

The first equality yields β=0\beta=0, which yields, together with the second equation m​y2+y+1=μ⋅(n​α2​y2+α​y+1)my^{2}+y+1=\mu\cdot(n\alpha^{2}y^{2}+\alpha y+1), so μ=1\mu=1, α=1\alpha=1 and thus m=nm=n, as we wanted. ∎

If char⁡(k)=p>0\mathrm{char}(\mathrm{k})=p>0, Lemma 3.7 only gives pp non-equivalent curves having the same complement. We can get more curves applying Lemma 3.2 to polynomials of higher degree:

Lemma 3.8.

For each integer n≥1n\geq 1 there exist curves C1,…,Cn⊂𝔸2C_{1},\dots,C_{n}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, all isomorphic to 𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0\}, no two being equivalent, such that all surfaces 𝔸2∖C1{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{1}, …\dots, 𝔸2∖Cn{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C_{n} are isomorphic.

Proof.

The case where char⁡(k)=0\mathrm{char}(\mathrm{k})=0 is provided by Lemma 3.7 so we can assume that char⁡(k)=p≥2\mathrm{char}(\mathrm{k})=p\geq 2. Set d=pn+2d=p^{n}+2. For each integer ii satisfying 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, there exists a unique polynomial Pi∈k⁡[y]P_{i}\in\mathrm{k}[y] of degree at most d−2=pnd-2=p^{n} satisfying

(D) Pi​(y)≡(1+y​Pi​(y))pi(modyd−1).P_{i}(y)\equiv\big(1+yP_{i}(y)\big)^{p^{i}}\pmod{y^{d-1}}.

Actually, the coefficients of PiP_{i} are inductively determined: Setting y=0y=0 in (D), we get Pi​(0)=1P_{i}(0)=1; assuming that the first mm coefficients u0,…,um−1u_{0},\ldots,u_{m-1} of Pi=∑j=0d−2uj​yjP_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{d-2}u_{j}y^{j} are known, Equation (D) yields us

∑j=0muj​yj≡(1+y​∑j=0m−1uj​yj)pi(modym+1)\sum_{j=0}^{m}u_{j}y^{j}\equiv\big(1+y\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}u_{j}y^{j})^{p^{i}}\pmod{y^{m+1}}

which determines umu_{m} in terms of u0,…,um−1u_{0},\ldots,u_{m-1}. In particular, for m=pim=p^{i}, we have

∑j=0piuj​yj≡1+ypi​(∑j=0pi−1uj​yj)pi≡1+ypi(modypi+1)\sum_{j=0}^{p^{i}}u_{j}y^{j}\equiv 1+y^{p^{i}}\big(\sum_{j=0}^{p^{i}-1}u_{j}y^{j})^{p^{i}}\equiv 1+y^{p^{i}}\pmod{y^{p^{i}+1}}

showing that Pi=1+ypi+(terms of higher order)P_{i}=1+y^{p^{i}}+\text{(terms of higher order)}. In fact, we could show that

Pi=1+∑kypk​i,P_{i}=1+\sum_{k}y^{p^{ki}},

where the sum is taken over all odd integers kk satisfying 0≤k​i≤n0\leq ki\leq n, but we will not need this result. As in Lemma 3.4, for each polynomial P∈k⁡[x]P\in\mathrm{k}[x], denote by CP⊂𝔸2C_{P}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} the closed curve given by the equation

x​yd+y​P​(y)+1=0.xy^{d}+yP(y)+1=0.

By Lemma 3.4(1) applied with (P,Q)=(Pi,1)(P,Q)=(P_{i},1) and m=pim=p^{i}, the curves CPiC_{P_{i}} and C1C_{1} of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} have isomorphic complements. To show that the curves CPiC_{P_{i}}, 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n are pairwise non-equivalent, we apply Lemma 3.2(2): for i,j∈{1,…,n}i,j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, the curves CPiC_{P_{i}} and CPjC_{P_{j}} are equivalent only if there exist α,λ,μ∈k∗\alpha,\lambda,\mu\in\mathrm{k}^{*}, β∈k\beta\in\mathrm{k} such that

yd=λ⋅(α​y+β)d,y​Pj​(y)+1=μ⋅((α​y+β)​Pi​(α​y+β)+1).y^{d}=\lambda\cdot(\alpha y+\beta)^{d},\quad yP_{j}(y)+1=\mu\cdot\big((\alpha y+\beta)P_{i}(\alpha y+\beta)+1\big).

The first equality yields β=0\beta=0. Replacing in the second equation, we get y​Pj​(y)+1=μ⁡(α​y​Pi​(α​y)+1)yP_{j}(y)+1=\mu\big(\alpha yP_{i}(\alpha y)+1\big), which is equivalent to μ=1\mu=1 and Pj​(y)=α​Pi​(α​y)P_{j}(y)=\alpha P_{i}(\alpha y). Setting y=0y=0, this gives us α=1\alpha=1. Therefore, we get Pj=PiP_{j}=P_{i}, so that i=ji=j, as we wanted. ∎

The proof of Theorem 2 is now finished:

Proof of Theorem 2.

Part (1) corresponds to Corollary 3.6. Part (2) is given by Corollary 3.7 (char⁡(k)=0\mathrm{char}(\mathrm{k})=0) and Lemma 3.8 (char⁡(k)>0\mathrm{char}(\mathrm{k})>0). Part (3) corresponds to Corollary 3.3. ∎

4. Non-isomorphic curves with isomorphic complements

4.1. A geometric construction

Proposition 4.1.

Proof.

Blowing up the singular point q1q_{1} of Γ\Gamma, the strict transform is isomorphic to ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} and intersects the exceptional divisor in one point (corresponding to the tangent direction given by the line RR), being tangent of the order d−1d-1. Hence, all points q2,…,qdq_{2},\dots,q_{d} belong to the strict transform of the exceptional divisor of q1q_{1}. This gives the self-intersections of ℱ1,…,ℱd\mathcal{F}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{F}_{d} and their configurations, as in the above diagram. As p1p_{1} is a smooth point of Γ\Gamma, the curves ℰ1,…,ℰd−1\mathcal{E}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{E}_{d-1} form a chain of curves as above. The rest of the diagram is checked by looking at the definitions of the curves Δ,Γ,L,R\Delta,\Gamma,L,R.

Let us write B=L~∪⋃i=1d−2ℰi∪⋃i=1dℱiB=\tilde{L}\cup\bigcup\limits_{i=1}^{d-2}\mathcal{E}_{i}\cup\bigcup\limits_{i=1}^{d}\mathcal{F}_{i}. In order to prove the result, one only needs to show the existence of isomorphisms

such that C=ψ1​(Γ~∖(B∪Δ~))C=\psi_{1}(\tilde{\Gamma}\setminus(B\cup\tilde{\Delta})) and D=ψ2​(Δ~∖(B∪Γ~))D=\psi_{2}(\tilde{\Delta}\setminus(B\cup\tilde{\Gamma})) are of degree d2−d+1d^{2}-d+1. Indeed, the existence of ψ1,ψ2\psi_{1},\psi_{2} implies that 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C and 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D are isomorphic, and that CC and DD are respectively isomorphic to Γ~∖(B∪Δ~)\tilde{\Gamma}\setminus(B\cup\tilde{\Delta}) and Δ~∖(B∪Γ~)\tilde{\Delta}\setminus(B\cup\tilde{\Gamma}). The morphism π\pi gives then isomorphisms of these curves with Γ∖(Δ∪{q})\Gamma\setminus(\Delta\cup\{q\}) and Δ∖(Γ∪L)\Delta\setminus(\Gamma\cup L) respectively.

We first show that ψ1\psi_{1} exists. We observe that since π\pi is the blow-up of 2​d−12d-1 k\mathrm{k}-points, the Picard group of XX is of rank 2​d2d, over k\mathrm{k} and over its algebraic closure k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}. The self-intersection is then (d2−d+1)+(d−1)⋅d2+(d−1)⋅(d−1)2+((d−1)2)2=(d2−d+1)2,(d^{2}-d+1)+(d-1)\cdot d^{2}+(d-1)\cdot(d-1)^{2}+((d-1)^{2})^{2}=(d^{2}-d+1)^{2}, which implies that the curve has degree d2−d+1d^{2}-d+1.

Corollary 4.2.

For each polynomial P∈k⁡[t]P\in\mathrm{k}[t] of degree d≥1d\geq 1 and each λ∈k\lambda\in\mathrm{k} with P⁡(λ)≠0P(\lambda)\not=0, there are two closed curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} of degree d2−d+1d^{2}-d+1 such that 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C and 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D are isomorphic and such that C≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])C\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}]) and D≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1Q])D\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}]), where Q⁡(t)=P⁡(λ+1t)⋅tdeg⁡(P)Q(t)=P(\lambda+\frac{1}{t})\cdot t^{\deg(P)}.

Proof.

Write Pd​(x,y)=P⁡(xy)​yd∈k⁡[x,y]P_{d}(x,y)=P(\frac{x}{y})y^{d}\in\mathrm{k}[x,y], which is a homogeneous polynomial of degree dd, such that Pd​(x,1)=P​(x)P_{d}(x,1)=P(x). We then choose Γ,Δ,L⊂ℙ2\Gamma,\Delta,L\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{2} to be the curve given by the following equations

Γ:yd−1​z=Pd​(x,y),Δ:z=0,L:x=λ​y.\Gamma:y^{d-1}z=P_{d}(x,y),\ \ \Delta:z=0,\ \ L:x=\lambda y.

By construction, PdP_{d} is not divisible by yy, so Γ\Gamma is irreducible and singular at q=[0:0:1]q=[0:0:1]. Moreover, the two lines LL and Δ\Delta satisfy L∩Γ={p1,q}L\cap\Gamma=\{p_{1},q\} where p1=[λ:1:P(λ)]p_{1}=[\lambda:1:P(\lambda)] and Δ\Delta does not pass through p1p_{1} or qq.

We apply Proposition 4.1, and obtain an isomorphism 𝔸2∖C≃𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\simeq{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D, where C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} are closed curves isomorphic to Γ∖(Δ∪{q})\Gamma\setminus(\Delta\cup\{q\}) and Δ∖(Γ∪L)\Delta\setminus(\Gamma\cup L) respectively and both have degree d2−d+1d^{2}-d+1.

Since Γ∖{q}\Gamma\setminus\{q\} is isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} via t↦[t:1:Pd(t,1)]=[t:1:P(t)]t\mapsto[t:1:P_{d}(t,1)]=[t:1:P(t)], we obtain that C≃Γ∖(Δ∪{q})C\simeq\Gamma\setminus(\Delta\cup\{q\}) is isomorphic to Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}]).

We then take the isomorphism 𝔸1→Δ∖L=Δ∖{[λ:1:0]}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to\Delta\setminus L=\Delta\setminus\{[\lambda:1:0]\} given by t↦[λt+1:t:0]t\mapsto[\lambda t+1:t:0]. The pull-back of Δ∩Γ\Delta\cap\Gamma corresponds to the zeroes of Pd​(λ​t+1,t)=td​Pd​(λ+1t,1)=Q⁡(t)P_{d}(\lambda t+1,t)=t^{d}P_{d}(\lambda+\frac{1}{t},1)=Q(t). Hence, DD is isomorphic to Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1Q])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}]) as desired. ∎

Corollary 4.3.

For each d≥1d\geq 1 and each distinct μ1,…,μd,λ∈k\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d},\lambda\in\mathrm{k}, there are two closed curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} such that 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C and 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D are isomorphic and such that C≃𝔸1∖{μ1,…,μd}C\simeq{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}\} and D≃ℙ1∖{[μ1:1],…,[μd:1],[λ:1]}D\simeq{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus\{[\mu_{1}:1],\dots,[\mu_{d}:1],[\lambda:1]\}.

Proof.

We apply Corollary 4.2 with P=∏i=1d(t−μi)P=\prod_{i=1}^{d}(t-\mu_{i}) and get two closed curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} such that 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C and 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D are isomorphic and such that C≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])≃𝔸1∖{μ1,…,μd}C\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}])\simeq{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{d}\} and D≃Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1Q])D\simeq\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}]), where Q⁡(t)=P⁡(λ+1t)⋅tdQ(t)=P(\lambda+\frac{1}{t})\cdot t^{d}. It remains to see that DD is isomorphic to ℙ1∖{[μ1:1],…,[μd:1],[λ:1]}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus\{[\mu_{1}:1],\dots,[\mu_{d}:1],[\lambda:1]\} via t↦[λt+1:t]t\mapsto[\lambda t+1:t]. ∎

Corollary 4.4.

If k\mathrm{k} is infinite and P∈k⁡[t]P\in\mathrm{k}[t] is a polynomial having at least 33 roots in k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}, then Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}]) and Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1Q])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}]) are not isomorphic, when Q⁡(t)=P⁡(λ+1t)⋅tdeg⁡(P)Q(t)=P(\lambda+\frac{1}{t})\cdot t^{\deg(P)} and λ∈k\lambda\in\mathrm{k} is a general element.

In particular, we can find two curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} having isomorphic complements, such that CC is isomorphic to Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}]) but not DD.

Proof.

Let λ1,…,λd∈k¯\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}\in\overline{\mathrm{k}} be the single roots of PP. It is enough to check that for a general λ\lambda, there exists no automorphism of ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} sending {λ1,…,λd,∞}\{\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d},\infty\} to {1λ1−λ,…,1λd−λ,∞}\{\frac{1}{\lambda_{1}-\lambda},\ldots,\frac{1}{\lambda_{d}-\lambda},\infty\}, or equivalently no automorphism sending {λ1,…,λd,∞}\{\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d},\infty\} to {λ1,…,λd,λ}\{\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d},\lambda\}. An automorphism of ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} being determined by the image of 3 points, the set 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} of automorphisms φ\varphi such that φ−1​({λ1,λ2,λ3})⊂{λ1,…,λd,∞}\varphi^{-1}(\{\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}\})\subset\{\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d},\infty\} has at most 6​(d+13)=(d+1)​d​(d−1)6{d+1\choose 3}=(d+1)d(d-1) elements. If λ\lambda does not belong to the following set

Λ={φ⁡(μ),φ∈𝒜,μ∈{λ1,…,λd,∞}},\Lambda=\{\varphi(\mu),\;\varphi\in{\mathcal{A}},\;\mu\in\{\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d},\infty\}\},

then no automorphism of ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} sends {λ1,…,λd,∞}\{\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d},\infty\} to {λ1,…,λd,λ}\{\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d},\lambda\}. This gives the result, together with Corollary 4.2. ∎

Remark 4.5.

If k\mathrm{k} is a finite field (with at least 33 elements), then the above result is false, by taking P=∏α∈k(x−α)P=\prod\limits_{\alpha\in\mathrm{k}}(x-\alpha). Indeed, if C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} are two curves such that CC is isomorphic to Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1P])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}]) and 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C is isomorphic to 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D, then DD is isomorphic to Spec⁡(k⁡[t,1Q])\Spec(\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}]) for some polynomial QQ without square factors having the same number of roots in k\mathrm{k} and in k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}} as PP (Theorem 1(2)). This implies that QQ is equal to μ​P\mu P for some μ∈k∗\mu\in\mathrm{k}^{*} and thus that CC and DD are isomorphic.

A similar argument holds for P=∏α∈k∗(x−α)P=\prod\limits_{\alpha\in\mathrm{k}^{*}}(x-\alpha) and P=∏α∈k∖{0,1}(x−α)P=\prod\limits_{\alpha\in\mathrm{k}\setminus\{0,1\}}(x-\alpha) (when the field has at least 44, respectively 55 elements).

Corollary 4.6.

For each ground field k\mathrm{k} having more than 2727 elements, one gets two geometrically irreducible curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} of degree 77 which are not isomorphic but such that 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C and 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D are isomorphic.

Proof.

We fix some ζ∈k∖{0,1}\zeta\in\mathrm{k}\setminus\{0,1\}. For each λ∈k∖{0,1,ζ}\lambda\in\mathrm{k}\setminus\{0,1,\zeta\}, one can apply Corollary 4.3 with d=3d=3, μ1=0,μ2=1,μ3=ζ\mu_{1}=0,\mu_{2}=1,\mu_{3}=\zeta and get two closed curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} such that 𝔸2∖C{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C and 𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D are isomorphic and such that C≃𝔸1∖{0,1,ζ}=ℙ1∖{[0:1],[1:1],[ζ:1],[1:0]}C\simeq{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\setminus\{0,1,\zeta\}={\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus\{[0:1],[1:1],[\zeta:1],[1:0]\} and D≃ℙ1∖{[0:1],[1:1],[ζ:1],[λ:1]}D\simeq{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\setminus\{[0:1],[1:1],[\zeta:1],[\lambda:1]\}. It remains to see that one can find at least one λ\lambda such that CC and DD are not isomorphic. Note that CC and DD are isomorphic if and only if there is an element of Aut⁡(ℙ1)=PGL2⁡(k)\Aut({\mathbb{P}}^{1})=\PGL_{2}(\mathrm{k}) that sends {[0:1],[1:1],[ζ:1],[λ:1]}\{[0:1],[1:1],[\zeta:1],[\lambda:1]\} onto {[0:1],[1:1],[ζ:1],[1:0]}\{[0:1],[1:1],[\zeta:1],[1:0]\}. The image of this element is determined by the image of [0:1],[1:1],[ζ:1][0:1],[1:1],[\zeta:1], so one gets at most 2424 automorphisms to avoid, hence at most 2424 elements of k∖{0,1,ζ}\mathrm{k}\setminus\{0,1,\zeta\} to avoid. The field k\mathrm{k} having at least 2828 elements, we find at least one λ\lambda having the right property. ∎

We can now give the proof of Theorem 3.

Proof of Theorem 3.

If the field is infinite (or simply more than 2727 elements), it follows from Corollary 4.6. Let us therefore assume that k\mathrm{k} is a finite field. We again apply Corollary 4.2 (with λ=0\lambda=0). Therefore, if |k|>2|\mathrm{k}|>2 (resp. |k|=2|\mathrm{k}|=2), it is enough to give a polynomial P∈k⁡[t]P\in\mathrm{k}[t] of degree 33 (resp. 44) such that P⁡(0)≠0P(0)\neq 0 and such that if we set Q:=P⁡(1t)​tdeg⁡PQ:=P(\frac{1}{t})t^{\deg P}, then the k\mathrm{k}-algebras k⁡[t,1P]\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}] and k⁡[t,1Q]\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}] are not isomorphic.

We begin with the case where the characteristic of k\mathrm{k} is odd. Then, the kernel of the morphism of groups k∗→k∗\mathrm{k}^{*}\to\mathrm{k}^{*}, x↦x2x\mapsto x^{2} is equal to {−1,1}\{-1,1\}, so that this map is not surjective. Let us pick an element α∈k∗∖(k∗)2\alpha\in\mathrm{k}^{*}\setminus(\mathrm{k}^{*})^{2}. Let us check that we can take P=(t−1)​((t−1)2−α)P=(t-1)((t-1)^{2}-\alpha). Indeed, up to a multiplicative constant, we have Q=(t−1)​((t−1)2−α​t2)Q=(t-1)((t-1)^{2}-\alpha t^{2}). Let us assume by contradiction that the algebras k⁡[t,1P]\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}] and k⁡[t,1Q]\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}] are isomorphic. Then, these algebras would still be isomorphic if we replace PP and QQ by

P~=P⁡(t+1)=t⁡(t2−α)​and​Q~=Q⁡(t+1)=t⁡(t2−α​(t+1)2).\tilde{P}=P(t+1)=t\big(t^{2}-\alpha\big)\;\text{and}\;\tilde{Q}=Q(t+1)=t\big(t^{2}-\alpha(t+1)^{2}\big).

This would yield an automorphism of ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}, via the embedding t↦[t:1]t\mapsto[t:1], which sends the polynomial u​v​(u2−α​v2)uv(u^{2}-\alpha v^{2}) onto u​v​(u2−α​(u+v)2)uv(u^{2}-\alpha(u+v)^{2}). This automorphism preserving the set of k\mathrm{k}-roots: {[0:1],[1:0]}\{[0:1],[1:0]\}, it is either of the form [u:v]↦[μu:v][u:v]\mapsto[\mu u:v] or [u:v]↦[μv:u][u:v]\mapsto[\mu v:u] where μ∈k∗\mu\in\mathrm{k}^{*}. The polynomial u2−α​v2u^{2}-\alpha v^{2} has to be sent to u2−α​(u+v)2u^{2}-\alpha(u+v)^{2}, which is not possible because of the term u​vuv.

We now handle the case where k\mathrm{k} has characteristic 22. We divide into three cases, depending wether the cube homomorphism of groups k∗→k∗\mathrm{k}^{*}\to\mathrm{k}^{*}, x↦x3x\mapsto x^{3} is injective or not (which corresponds to ask if 44 divides |k|\lvert\mathrm{k}\rvert or not), and putting the field with two elements apart.

If the cube homomorphism is not surjective, we can pick an element α∈k∗∖(k∗)3\alpha\in\mathrm{k}^{*}\setminus(\mathrm{k}^{*})^{3}. Let us check that we can take the irreducible polynomial P=t3−α∈k⁡[t]P=t^{3}-\alpha\in\mathrm{k}[t]. Indeed, up to a multiplicative constant, we have Q=t3−α−1Q=t^{3}-\alpha^{-1}. Let us assume by contradiction that the algebras k⁡[t,1P]\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}] and k⁡[t,1Q]\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}] are isomorphic. Then, there should exist constants λ,μ,c∈k\lambda,\mu,c\in\mathrm{k} with λ​c≠0\lambda c\neq 0 such that

c⁡(t3−α−1)=(λ​t+μ)3−α.c(t^{3}-\alpha^{-1})=(\lambda t+\mu)^{3}-\alpha.

This gives us μ=0\mu=0 and λ3=c=α2\lambda^{3}=c=\alpha^{2}. The square homomorphism of groups k∗→k∗\mathrm{k}^{*}\to\mathrm{k}^{*}, x↦x2x\mapsto x^{2} being bijective, there is a unique square root for each element of k∗\mathrm{k}^{*}. Taking the square root of the equality α2=λ3\alpha^{2}=\lambda^{3}, we obtain α=(ν)3\alpha=(\nu)^{3}, where ν\nu is the square root of λ\lambda. This is impossible since α\alpha was chosen not to be a cube.

If the cube homomorphism is surjective, then 11 is the only root of t3−1=(t−1)​(t2+t+1)t^{3}-1=(t-1)(t^{2}+t+1), so t2+t+1∈k⁡[t]t^{2}+t+1\in\mathrm{k}[t] is irrreducible. If moreover k\mathrm{k} has more than 22 elements, we can choose α∈k∖{0,1}\alpha\in\mathrm{k}\setminus\{0,1\} and take P=(t−α)​(t2+t+1)P=(t-\alpha)(t^{2}+t+1). Up to a multiplicative constant, we have Q=(t−α−1)​(t2+t+1)Q=(t-\alpha^{-1})(t^{2}+t+1). Let us assume by contradiction that the algebras k⁡[t,1P]\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}] and k⁡[t,1Q]\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}] are isomorphic. Then, these algebras would still be isomorphic if we replace PP and QQ by

P~=P⁡(t+α)=t⁡(t2+t+α2+α+1)​and​Q~=Q⁡(t+α−1)=t⁡(t2+t+α−2+α−1+1).\tilde{P}=P(t+\alpha)=t(t^{2}+t+\alpha^{2}+\alpha+1)\;\text{and}\;\tilde{Q}=Q(t+\alpha^{-1})=t(t^{2}+t+\alpha^{-2}+\alpha^{-1}+1).

This would yield an automorphism of ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}, via the embedding t↦[t:1]t\mapsto[t:1], which sends the polynomial u​v​(u2+u​v+(α2+α+1)​v2)uv(u^{2}+uv+(\alpha^{2}+\alpha+1)v^{2}) onto u​v​(u2+u​v+(α−2+α−1+1)​v2)uv(u^{2}+uv+(\alpha^{-2}+\alpha^{-1}+1)v^{2}). The same argument as before yields α2+α+1=α−2+α−1+1\alpha^{2}+\alpha+1=\alpha^{-2}+\alpha^{-1}+1, i.e. α2+α+1=α−2​(α2+α+1)\alpha^{2}+\alpha+1=\alpha^{-2}(\alpha^{2}+\alpha+1). This is impossible since α2+α+1≠0\alpha^{2}+\alpha+1\neq 0 and α2≠1\alpha^{2}\neq 1.

The last case is when k={0,1}\mathrm{k}=\{0,1\} is the field with two elements. Here the construction does not work with polynomials of degree 33: the only ones which are not symmetric and do not vanish in 00 are t3+t2+1t^{3}+t^{2}+1 and t3+t+1t^{3}+t+1, which are equivalent via t↦t+1t\mapsto t+1. We then choose for PP the irreducible polynomial P=t4+t+1P=t^{4}+t+1 (it has not root and is not equal to (t2+t+1)2=t4+t2+1(t^{2}+t+1)^{2}=t^{4}+t^{2}+1). This gives Q=t4+t3+1Q=t^{4}+t^{3}+1. Let us assume by contradiction that the algebras k⁡[t,1P]\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{P}] and k⁡[t,1Q]\mathrm{k}[t,\frac{1}{Q}] are isomorphic. Then, there should exist constants λ,μ,c∈k\lambda,\mu,c\in\mathrm{k} with λ​c≠0\lambda c\neq 0 such that

c⁡(t4+t3+1)=(λ​t+μ)4+(λ​t+μ)+1.c(t^{4}+t^{3}+1)=(\lambda t+\mu)^{4}+(\lambda t+\mu)+1.

This is impossible since (λ​t+μ)4+(λ​t+μ)+1=λ4​t4+λ​t+(μ4+μ+1)(\lambda t+\mu)^{4}+(\lambda t+\mu)+1=\lambda^{4}t^{4}+\lambda t+(\mu^{4}+\mu+1). ∎

4.2. Getting explicit formulas

To obtain the equation of the curves C,DC,D and the isomorphism 𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D given by Proposition 4.1, one can follow the construction and explicit the birational maps described. The lemma yields the existence of isomorphisms

ψ1:X∖(B∪Δ~)⟶≃𝔸2​ and ​ψ2:X∖(B∪Γ~)⟶≃𝔸2\psi_{1}\colon X\setminus(B\cup\tilde{\Delta})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\mbox{ and }\psi_{2}\colon X\setminus(B\cup\tilde{\Gamma})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}

such that C=ψ1​(Γ~∖(B∪Δ~))C=\psi_{1}(\tilde{\Gamma}\setminus(B\cup\tilde{\Delta})) and D=ψ2​(Δ~∖(B∪Γ~))D=\psi_{2}(\tilde{\Delta}\setminus(B\cup\tilde{\Gamma})) are of degree d2−d+1d^{2}-d+1, where B=L~∪⋃i=1d−2ℰi∪⋃i=1dℱiB=\tilde{L}\cup\bigcup\limits_{i=1}^{d-2}\mathcal{E}_{i}\cup\bigcup\limits_{i=1}^{d}\mathcal{F}_{i}, and ψ1,ψ2\psi_{1},\psi_{2} are given by blow-ups and blow-downs, so it is possible to explicit ψi​π−1:ℙ2⇢ℙ2\psi_{i}\pi^{-1}\colon{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2} with formulas (looking at the linear systems), and then get the isomorphism ψ2​π−1∘(ψ1​π−1)−1:𝔸2∖C→𝔸2∖D\psi_{2}\pi^{-1}\circ(\psi_{1}\pi^{-1})^{-1}\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D. The formulas for ψ1​π−1,ψ2​π−1\psi_{1}\pi^{-1},\psi_{2}\pi^{-1} are however quite complicated.

Another possibility can be done as follows: we choose a birational morphism X→WX\to W that contracts L~,ℰ1,…,ℰd−2\tilde{L},\mathcal{E}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{E}_{d-2} and ℱd,…,ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{d},\dots,\mathcal{F}_{2} onto two smooth points of WW, passing through the image of ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1} (possible, see Diagram (E)). The situation of the image of the curves R~,ℰd−1,ℱ1,Γ~,Δ~\tilde{R},\mathcal{E}_{d-1},\mathcal{F}_{1},\tilde{\Gamma},\tilde{\Delta} (that we again denote by the same name) in WW is as follows:

Computing the dimension of the Picard group, one finds that WW is a Hirzebruch surface. Hence, the curves ℰd−1,R~\mathcal{E}_{d-1},\tilde{R} are fibres of a ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-bundle W→ℙ1W\to{\mathbb{P}}^{1} and ℱ1,Δ~,Γ~\mathcal{F}_{1},\tilde{\Delta},\tilde{\Gamma} are sections of self-intersection d−2,d,dd-2,d,d. One can then find plenty of examples in 𝔽1\mathbb{F}_{1} and 𝔽0\mathbb{F}_{0} (depending on the parity of dd) but also in 𝔽m\mathbb{F}_{m} for m≥2m\geq 2 if the polynomial chosen at the beginning is special enough.

The case where d=3d=3 corresponds to curves of degree 77 in 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} (Proposition 4.1) which is the first interesting case, as it gives non-isomorphic curves for almost each field (Theorem 3). When d=3d=3, one finds that ℱ1\mathcal{F}_{1} is a section of self-intersection 11 in W=𝔽1W=\mathbb{F}_{1}, so 𝔽1∖ℱ1\mathbb{F}_{1}\setminus\mathcal{F}_{1} is isomorphic to the blow-up of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} at one point, and Γ~,Δ~\tilde{\Gamma},\tilde{\Delta} are sections of self-intersecion 33 and are thus strict transforms of parabolas passing through the point blown up. This explains how the following result is derived from Proposition 4.1. However, the result can also be read independently of Proposition 4.1, since the proof that we give does not use the rest of the article:

By construction, (ψQ)−1​(Cμ)(\psi_{Q})^{-1}(C_{\mu}) is equal to Γ~μ∖Δ~\tilde{\Gamma}_{\mu}\setminus\tilde{\Delta}, where Γ~μ⊂𝔸^2\tilde{\Gamma}_{\mu}\subset\hat{{\mathbb{A}}}^{2} is the strict transform of the curve Γμ⊂𝔸2\Gamma_{\mu}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} given by (a0)2​P−μ​Q=0(a_{0})^{2}P-\mu Q=0 (follows from Equation (F)). The closure of Γμ\Gamma_{\mu} in ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} is a conic given by

(a0)2​x2−μ​y2−z⁡(a0​(μ+a0​a2)​x−(μ​a1+(a0)2​a3)​y)(a_{0})^{2}x^{2}-\mu y^{2}-z(a_{0}(\mu+a_{0}a_{2})x-(\mu a_{1}+(a_{0})^{2}a_{3})y)

which passes through [0:0:1][0:0:1] and is irreducible for a general μ\mu. Projecting from the point one obtains an isomorphism with ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}. The curve Γ~μ∖Δ~\tilde{\Gamma}_{\mu}\setminus\tilde{\Delta} is then isomorphic to ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} minus three k¯\overline{\mathrm{k}}-points of Δ~\tilde{\Delta}, which are fixed and do not depend on μ\mu, and minus the two points at infinity, which correspond to (a0)2​x2−μ​y2=0(a_{0})^{2}x^{2}-\mu y^{2}=0.

When the field is algebraically closed, one thus gets that the general fibres of ff are isomorphic to ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} minus 44 points, whereas the zero fibre is isomorphic to ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} minus 33 points (if ∑i=03ai​ti\sum_{i=0}^{3}a_{i}t^{i} is chosen to have three distint roots). Moreover, the two points of intersection with the line at infinity say that this curve is a horizontal curve of degree 22, or equivalently a horizontal curve which is not a section (in the usual notation of polynomials and components on boundary, see [NN02, AC96]), so the polynomials ff and gg are rational but not of simple type (see [NN02]). When k=ℂ\mathrm{k}={\mathbb{C}}, this implies that the polynomial has non-trivial monodromy [ACD98].

5. Related questions

5.1. Providing higher dimensional counterexamples

As one now explains, the negative answer to the Complement Problem for n=2n=2 also yields a negative answer for any n≥3n\geq 3. This follows from the following easy observation:

Lemma 5.1.

Let C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} be two closed geometrically irreducible curves having isomorphic complements. Then for each m≥1m\geq 1, the varieties HC=C×𝔸mH_{C}=C\times{\mathbb{A}}^{m} and HD=D×𝔸mH_{D}=D\times{\mathbb{A}}^{m} are closed hypersurfaces of 𝔸2×𝔸m=𝔸m+2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{m}={\mathbb{A}}^{m+2} having isomorphic complements. Moreover, CC and DD are isomorphic if and only if C×𝔸mC\times{\mathbb{A}}^{m} and D×𝔸mD\times{\mathbb{A}}^{m} are isomorphic.

Proof.

Denoting by f,g∈k⁡[x,y]f,g\in\mathrm{k}[x,y] the geometrically irreducible polynomials that define the curves C,DC,D, the varieties HC,HD⊂𝔸2×𝔸m=𝔸m+2H_{C},H_{D}\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{m}={\mathbb{A}}^{m+2} are given by the same polynomials and are thus again closed geometrically irreducible hypersurfaces. The isomorphism 𝔸2∖C⟶≃𝔸2∖D{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus C\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\setminus D extends then naturally to an isomorphism 𝔸m+2∖HC⟶≃𝔸m+2∖HD{\mathbb{A}}^{m+2}\setminus H_{C}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\simeq}}{{\longrightarrow}}{\mathbb{A}}^{m+2}\setminus H_{D}.

If CC and DD are isomorphic, then HCH_{C} and HDH_{D} are isomorphic. The converse also holds, and is proven in [AHE72, Corollary (3.4)]. ∎

Corollary 5.2.

For each ground field k\mathrm{k} and each integer n≥3n\geq 3, there exist two geometrically irreducible smooth closed hypersurfaces E,F⊂𝔸nE,F\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{n} which are not isomorphic but whose complements 𝔸n∖E{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\setminus E and 𝔸n∖F{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\setminus F are isomorphic. Furthermore, the hypersurfaces can be given by polynomials f,g∈k⁡[x1,x2]⊂k⁡[x1,…,xn]f,g\in\mathrm{k}[x_{1},x_{2}]\subset\mathrm{k}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}] of degree 77 if the field admits strictly more than 22 elements and of degree 1313 if the field has 22 elements. The hypersurfaces E,FE,F are isomorphic to C×𝔸n−2C\times{\mathbb{A}}^{n-2} and D×𝔸n−2D\times{\mathbb{A}}^{n-2} for some smooth closed curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} of the same degree.

Proof.

It suffices to choose for f,gf,g the equations of the curves C,D⊂𝔸2C,D\subset{\mathbb{A}}^{2} given by Theorem 3. The result then follows from Lemma 5.1. ∎

5.2. The holomorphic case

Lemma 5.3.

For each d+1d+1 distinct points a1,…,ad,ad+1∈ℂa_{1},\dots,a_{d},a_{d+1}\in{\mathbb{C}}, with d≥3d\geq 3, there exist two closed algebraic curves C,D⊂ℂ2C,D\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{2} of degree d2−d+1d^{2}-d+1 such that CC and DD are algebraically isomorphic to ℂ∖{a1,…,ad−1,ad}{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\{a_{1},\dots,a_{d-1},a_{d}\} and ℂ∖{a1,…,ad−1,ad+1}{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\{a_{1},\dots,a_{d-1},a_{d+1}\} respectively, and such that ℂ2∖C{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\setminus C and ℂ2∖D{\mathbb{C}}^{2}\setminus D are algebraically isomorphic.

In particular, choosing the points generally enough, the curves CC and DD are not biholomorphic, but their complements are biholomorphic.

Proof.

The existence of C,DC,D directly follows from Corollary 4.2. It remains to observe that CC and DD are not biholomorphic if the points are general enough. If f:C→Df\colon C\to D is a biholomorphism, then ff extends to a holomorphic map ℂ​ℙ1→ℂ​ℙ1{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\to{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1}, as it cannot have essential singularities. The same holds for f−1f^{-1}, so ff is just an element of PGL2⁡(ℂ)\PGL_{2}({\mathbb{C}}), hence an algebraic automorphism of the projective complex line. Removing at least 44 points of ℂ​ℙ1{\mathbb{C}}{\mathbb{P}}^{1} (this is the case since d≥3d\geq 3) and moving one of them gives then infinitely many curves up to biholomorphism. ∎

Corollary 5.4.

For each n≥2n\geq 2, there are algebraic hypersurfaces H1,H2⊂ℂnH_{1},H_{2}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{n} which are complex manifolds, not biholomorphic but having biholomorphic complements.

Proof.

It suffices to take polynomials f,g∈ℂ⁡[x1,x2]f,g\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},x_{2}] provided by Lemma 5.3, whose zero sets are smooth algebraic curves C,D⊂ℂ2C,D\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{2} not biholomorphic but having holomorphic complements. We then use the same polynomials to define H1,H2⊂ℂnH_{1},H_{2}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, which are smooth complex manifolds having biholomorphic complements and being biholomorphic to C×ℂn−2C\times{\mathbb{C}}^{n-2} and D×ℂn−2D\times{\mathbb{C}}^{n-2} respectively. It remains to observe that C×ℂn−2C\times{\mathbb{C}}^{n-2} and D×ℂn−2D\times{\mathbb{C}}^{n-2} are not biholomorphic. Denote by pC:C×ℂn−2→Cp_{C}\colon C\times{\mathbb{C}}^{n-2}\to C and pD:D×ℂn−2→Dp_{D}\colon D\times{\mathbb{C}}^{n-2}\to D the projections on the first factor. If ψ:ℂn−2×C→ℂn−2×D\psi\colon{\mathbb{C}}^{n-2}\times C\to{\mathbb{C}}^{n-2}\times D is a biholomorphism, then pD∘ψ:ℂn−2×C→Dp_{D}\circ\psi\colon{\mathbb{C}}^{n-2}\times C\to D induces, for each c∈Cc\in C, a holomorphic map ℂn−2→D{\mathbb{C}}^{n-2}\to D which has to be constant by Picard’s theorem (since it avoids at least two values of ℂ{\mathbb{C}}). Therefore, the map pD∘ψp_{D}\circ\psi factors through a holomorphic map χ:C→D\chi\colon C\to D: we have pD∘φ=χ∘pCp_{D}\circ\varphi=\chi\circ p_{C}. We get analogously a holomorphic map θ:D→C\theta\colon D\to C, which is by construction the inverse of χ\chi, so CC and DD are biholomorphic, a contradiction. ∎

Appendix: The case of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}

In this appendix, we describe some results on the question of complements of curves in ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} explained in the introduction. These are not directly related to the rest of the text and only serve as comparison with the affine case.

We recall the following simple argument, known to specialists, for lack of reference:

Lemma 5.5.

Let C,D⊂ℙ2C,D\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{2} be two geometrically irreducible closed curves such that ℙ2∖C{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus C and ℙ2∖D{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus D are isomorphic. If CC and DD are not equivalent, up to automorphism of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, then CC and DD are singular rational curves.

Proof.

Denote by φ:ℙ2⇢ℙ2\varphi\colon{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\dasharrow{\mathbb{P}}^{2} a birational map which restricts to an isomorphism from ℙ2∖C{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus C to ℙ2∖D{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus D. If φ\varphi is an automorphism of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}, then CC and DD are equivalent. Otherwise, the same argument as in Lemma 2.7 shows that both CC and DD are rational (this also follows from [Bla09, Lemma 2.2]). If CC and DD are singular, we are finished, so we can assume that one of them is smooth, and then has degree 11 or 22. The Picard group of ℙ2∖C{\mathbb{P}}^{2}\setminus C being ℤ/deg⁡(C)​ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}/\deg(C){\mathbb{Z}}, one finds that CC and DD have the same degree. This implies that CC and DD are equivalent under automorphisms of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}. The case of lines is obvious. For conics, it is enough to check that a rational conic over any field is necessarily equivalent to the conic of equation x​y+z2=0xy+z^{2}=0. Actually, one may always assume that the rational conic contains the point [1:0:0][1:0:0], since it contains a rational point. One may furthermore assume that the tangent at this point has equation y=0y=0. This means that the equation of the conic is of the form x​y+u⁡(y,z)xy+u(y,z), where uu is a homogenous polynomial of degree 22. Using a change of variables of the form (x,y,z)↦(x+a​y+b​z,y,z)(x,y,z)\mapsto(x+ay+bz,y,z), where a,b∈ka,b\in\mathrm{k}, one may assume that the equation is of the form x​y+c​z2=0xy+cz^{2}=0, where c∈k∗c\in\mathrm{k}^{*}. Then, using the change of variables (x,y,z)↦(c​x,y,z)(x,y,z)\mapsto(cx,y,z), one finally gets, as announced, the equation x​y+z2=0xy+z^{2}=0. ∎

In order to get families of (singular) curves of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} having the same complement, we explicit here the construction of Paolo Costa [Cos12], that provides examples of unicuspidal curves of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} having isomorphic complements but being non-equivalent under the action of Aut⁡(ℙ2)\Aut({\mathbb{P}}^{2}). We provide equations and give the details of the proof for self-containedness, and because the results below are not explicitly stated in [Cos12].

To each homogeneous polynomial P∈k⁡[x,y]P\in\mathrm{k}[x,y] of degree d≥1d\geq 1, one associates a homogeneous irreducible polynomial fP∈k⁡[x,y,z]f_{P}\in\mathrm{k}[x,y,z] of degree 4​d+14d+1:

fP=z​(x​z−y2)2​d+2​y​P​(x2,x​z−y2)​(x​z−y2)d+x​(P⁡(x2,x​z−y2))2f_{P}=z(xz-y^{2})^{2d}+2yP(x^{2},xz-y^{2})(xz-y^{2})^{d}+x(P(x^{2},xz-y^{2}))^{2}

The construction of Lemma 5.6 yields, for each d≥1d\geq 1, families of curves of degree 4​d+14d+1 having the same complement. These are equivalent for d=1d=1, at least when k\mathrm{k} is algebraically closed (Lemma 5.6(4)), but not for d≥2d\geq 2. One can now easily provide explicit examples:

Corollary 5.7.

Let d≥2d\geq 2 be an integer, and let P=xd+xd−1​y∈k⁡[x,y]P=x^{d}+x^{d-1}y\in\mathrm{k}[x,y]. All curves of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} given by

z​(x​z−y2)2​d+2​y​P​(λ​x2,x​z−y2)​(x​z−y2)d+x​(P⁡(λ​x2,x​z−y2))2z(xz-y^{2})^{2d}+2yP(\lambda x^{2},xz-y^{2})(xz-y^{2})^{d}+x(P(\lambda x^{2},xz-y^{2}))^{2}

for λ∈k∗\lambda\in\mathrm{k}^{*}, have the same complement and are pairwise not equivalent, up to automorphism of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2}.

Proof.

The curves correspond to the curves CP⁡(λ​x,y)C_{P(\lambda x,y)} of Lemma 5.6 and have thus isomorphic complements by Lemma 5.6(3). It remains to show that if CP⁡(λ​x,y)C_{P(\lambda x,y)} is equivalent to CP⁡(λ~​x,y)C_{P(\tilde{\lambda}x,y)}, then λ=λ~\lambda=\tilde{\lambda}. Lemma 5.6(3) yields the existence of ρ∈k∗,μ∈k\rho\in\mathrm{k}^{*},\mu\in\mathrm{k} such that P⁡(λ~​x,y)=ρ​P​(ρ2​λ​x,y)+μ​ydP(\tilde{\lambda}x,y)=\rho P(\rho^{2}\lambda x,y)+\mu y^{d}. Since d≥2d\geq 2, both P⁡(λ~​x,y)P(\tilde{\lambda}x,y) and ρ​P​(x​ρ2​λ,y)\rho P(x\rho^{2}\lambda,y) do not have component with ydy^{d}, so μ=0\mu=0. We then compare the coefficients of xdx^{d} and xd−1​yx^{d-1}y and get

λ~d=ρ​(ρ2​λ)d,λ~d−1=ρ​(ρ2​λ)d−1,\tilde{\lambda}^{d}=\rho(\rho^{2}\lambda)^{d},\ \ \tilde{\lambda}^{d-1}=\rho(\rho^{2}\lambda)^{d-1},

which yields λ~=ρ2​λ\tilde{\lambda}=\rho^{2}\lambda, so λ~d=(ρ2​λ)d\tilde{\lambda}^{d}=(\rho^{2}\lambda)^{d}, whence ρ=1\rho=1 and λ~=λ\tilde{\lambda}=\lambda as desired. ∎
